Some understand by this stone Christ, the corner stone[[Eph 2:20||]], who at the judgment cries out against those who are to be damned, according to the saying in Isaias: [[Is 42:13|he shall shout and cry: he shall prevail against his enemies|Vociferabitur et clamabit, et super inimicos suos confortabitur]].

paras.t: Væ qui ædificat civitatem in sanguinibus, et præparat urbem in iniquitate. Hoc generaliter accipi potest adversus principes qui de prædis et sumptibus aliorum injustis construunt sibi urbes, domos et castra, inaniter et pompose. Aptius tamen accipitur contra prælatos carnales et aliorum seductores, qui Ecclesias suas vitiose gubernant, mendaciter instruunt, et in perditionem suam ac subditorum subvertunt.
paras.en: [[2:12|Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and prepareth a city by iniquity.|Væ qui ædificat civitatem in sanguinibus, et præparat urbem in iniquitate!]] This can be taken in general against princes who out of plunder and the unjust spending of other men's goods build themselves cities, houses and castles, vainly and with pomp. But it is more fitly taken against carnal prelates and the seducers of others, who govern their churches viciously, teach them falsely, and overthrow them to their own ruin and that of their subjects.

paras.t: Numquid non hæc sunt a Domino exercituum? id est, prædicta mala pœnalia, seu justæ vindictæ a Deo sunt utique, qui ait per Isaiam: Ego Dominus faciens bonum, et creans malum. Vel sensus est, quod ædificatio ista culpabilis non est a Deo, quantum ad deformitatem peccati. Quod autem ista non sint hoc modo a Deo, et quod quidam male ab aliis gubernentur, hinc patet: Laborabunt enim populi male recti atque seducti, in multo igne iræ, et cupiditatis, ac vitiorum, imo et igne tartareo; et gentes hujuscemodi in vacuum laborabunt, et deficient, id est, felicem finem non consequuntur, et fine frustrabuntur optato. Unde in libro Sapientiæ fatentur: Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles.
paras.en: [[2:13|Are not these things from the Lord of hosts|Numquid non hæc sunt a Domino exercituum]]? that is, the penal evils spoken of, or just punishments, are surely from God, who says through Isaias: I the Lord, [[Is 45:7|I make peace, and create evil|faciens bonum, et creans malum]] [Denis reads *bonum*, “good”; the edition notes the Vulgate's *pacem*, “peace”]. Or the sense is that this building is not from God, as regards the deformity of sin, for which it is blamed. And that these things are not from God in this way, and that some are badly governed by others, is plain from this: [[2:13|for the people shall labour|Laborabunt enim populi]], badly ruled and led astray, [[2:13|in a great fire|in multo igne]] of wrath, of greed and of vices, nay, in the fire of hell too; [[2:13|and the nations|et gentes]] of this kind shall labour [[2:13|in vain|in vacuum]], [[2:13|and they shall faint|et deficient]], that is, they do not reach a happy end, and will be cheated of the end they hoped for. Hence in the book of Wisdom they confess: [[Wis 5:7|We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked through hard ways|Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles]].

paras.t: Signum quoque veritatis istorum est, Quia replebitur terra, id est, Ecclesia electorum in hac valle miseriæ se ipsam semper humilians, a Spiritu Sancto unctionem et illustrationem suscipiet, ut cognoscat gloriam Domini, id est excellentiam sapientiæ atque justitiæ Dei, seu majestatem divinam, in justa punitione pravorum salvationeque electorum. Quod fiet tam copiose, quasi aquæ operientes mare, id est sicut flumina, quæ jugiter et exuberanter descendunt in mare Magnum, ejusque superficiem tangendo operiunt. Unde Ecclesiastes inducit: Ad locum unde exeunt flumina, revertuntur, ut iterum fluant. Et ibidem scriptum est: Omnia flumina intrant in mare, et mare non redundat. Denique huic simile est illud Isaiæ: Repleta est terra scientia Domini, sicut aquæ maris operientes.
paras.en: A sign of the truth of these things, too, is this: [[2:14|For the earth shall be filled|Quia replebitur terra]], that is, the Church of the elect, always humbling herself in this vale of misery, will receive anointing and enlightening from the Holy Ghost, [[2:14|that men may know the glory of the Lord|ut cognoscat gloriam Domini]] [Denis reads *cognoscat*, “that it may know”, where the Vulgate has *cognoscant*], that is, the excellence of God's wisdom and justice, or the divine majesty, in the just punishment of the wicked and the salvation of the elect. This will be done as abundantly [[2:14|as waters covering the sea|quasi aquæ operientes mare]], that is, like the rivers which flow down continually and abundantly into the Great Sea, and cover its surface as they touch it. Hence Ecclesiastes brings in: [[Eccles 1:7|unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return, to flow again|Ad locum unde exeunt flumina, revertuntur, ut iterum fluant]]. And it is written in the same place: [[Eccles 1:7|All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea doth not overflow|Omnia flumina intrant in mare, et mare non redundat]]. Lastly, like this is the saying of Isaias: [[Is 11:9|the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the covering waters of the sea|Repleta est terra scientia Domini, sicut aquæ maris operientes]].

paras.t: Væ qui potum dat amico suo, mittens fel suum, id est cuilibet adulatori seu deceptori, qui mala sub specie boni proponit, et vere nociva atque amara vel æternæ amaritudinis inductiva ingerit alteri, quem se confingit amare, ut adspiciat nuditatem ejus, id est, reddat eum confusum, et bonis privatum. Hinc Isaias: Fraudulenti, inquit, vasa pessima sunt; et Psalmista, Virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus. Sed et qui sophistice loquitur, odibilis est. Ideo ait Apostolus: Ab omni specie mala abstinete vos. Repletus est ignominia qui ita decipitur.
paras.en: [[2:15|Woe to him that giveth drink to his friend, and presenteth his gall|Væ qui potum dat amico suo, mittens fel suum]], that is, woe to any flatterer or deceiver, who puts forward evil things under the appearance of good, and forces on another, whom he pretends to love, things truly harmful and bitter, or leading to everlasting bitterness, [[2:15|that he may behold his nakedness|ut adspiciat nuditatem ejus]], that is, that he may leave him confounded and stripped of good things. Hence Isaias: [[Is 32:7|The vessels of the deceitful|Fraudulenti]], he says, [[Is 32:7|are most wicked|vasa pessima sunt]]; and the Psalmist, [[Ps 5:7|The bloody and the deceitful man the Lord will abhor|Virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus]]. And also, [[Ecclus 37:23|He that speaketh sophistically, is hateful|qui sophistice loquitur, odibilis est]]. Therefore the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 5:22|From all appearance of evil refrain yourselves.|Ab omni specie mala abstinete vos.]] He that is so deceived is [[2:16|filled with shame|Repletus est ignominia]] [Denis reads *Repletus est*, “he is filled”, where the Vulgate has *Repletus es*, “thou art filled”, and takes it of the deceived friend of v. 15].

paras.t: Bibe tu quoque, et consopire, id est, tu deceptor, vicissitudinem recipe, et quod meruisti, sustine. Circumdabit te calix dexteræ Domini, id est districta ultio Dei, quatenus sicut fecisti proximo, fiat tibi a Deo: quemadmodum Christus in Evangelio, Eadem, inquit, mensura qua mensi fueritis, remetietur vobis. Hinc Joannes in Apocalypsi testatus est: Hic bibet de vino iræ Dei omnipotentis, quod mixtum est mero in calice iræ ipsius. De calice isto habetur in Psalmo: Calix in manu Domini vini meri, plenus mixto; item in Jeremia: Calix aureus Babylon in manu Domini; de vino ejus bibent omnes gentes. Præterea advertendum, quod dextera Domini in Scripturis sæpe in bono accipitur: et tunc magnum gratiæ ejus favorem ac pietatem designat, sicut in Psalmo, quo dicitur, Dextera tua suscepit me. Interdum quoque in malo accipitur: tuncque designat gravem Dei vindictam, quemadmodum etiam homo gravius percutit dextera quam sinistra. Unde cantamus in Psalmo, Dextera tua inveniat omnes qui te oderunt; atque in loco præsenti, Circumdabit te calix dexteræ Domini. Et vomitus ignominiæ circumdabit te, id est, tanta a Deo confusione repleberis, ut præ crapula vomens quod sumpsit: quia iniquitas tua et justa punitio redundabit in te: sicut in Psalmo habetur, Lacum aperuit et effodit eum, et incidit in foveam quam fecit; in Proverbiorum quoque libro, In insidiis suis capientur iniqui. Et in Isaia legitur: Væ impio in malum; retributio manuum ejus fiet ei. Super gloriam tuam, id est post inanissimam gloriationem et frivolam exsultationem, quam in aliorum supplantatione habuisti. Hoc dicitur contra eos qui in aliorum ruina lætantur.
paras.en: [[2:16|drink thou also, and fall fast asleep|Bibe tu quoque, et consopire]], that is, thou deceiver, receive thy turn, and bear what thou hast deserved. [[2:16|the cup of the right hand of the Lord shall compass thee|Circumdabit te calix dexteræ Domini]], that is, the strict vengeance of God, so that as thou hast done to thy neighbour, so may it be done to thee by God: as Christ in the Gospel: [[Luke 6:38|with the same|Eadem]], he says, [[Luke 6:38|measure that you shall mete withal, it shall be measured to you again|mensura qua mensi fueritis, remetietur vobis]][[Matt 7:2||]]. Hence John testified in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 14:10|He also shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is mingled with pure wine in the cup of his wrath|Hic bibet de vino iræ Dei omnipotentis, quod mixtum est mero in calice iræ ipsius]] [Denis adds *omnipotentis*, “of the wrath of almighty God”]. Of this cup it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 74:9|in the hand of the Lord there is a cup of strong wine full of mixture|Calix in manu Domini vini meri, plenus mixto]]; and in Jeremias: [[Jer 51:7|Babylon hath been a golden cup in the hand of the Lord|Calix aureus Babylon in manu Domini]]; [[Jer 51:7|the nations have drunk of her wine|de vino ejus bibent omnes gentes]] [Denis reads “all nations shall drink of her wine”]. It should be noted further that *the right hand of the Lord* is often taken in a good sense in the Scriptures: and then it signifies the great favour and kindness of his grace, as in the Psalm where it is said, [[Ps 17:36|thy right hand hath held me up|Dextera tua suscepit me]]. Sometimes too it is taken in a bad sense, and then it signifies God's heavy vengeance, just as a man too strikes harder with the right hand than with the left. Hence we sing in the Psalm, [[Ps 20:9|let thy right hand find out all them that hate thee|Dextera tua inveniat omnes qui te oderunt]]; and in the present place, [[2:16|the cup of the right hand of the Lord shall compass thee|Circumdabit te calix dexteræ Domini]]. [[2:16|and shameful vomiting|Et vomitus ignominiæ]] shall compass thee, that is, thou shalt be filled with such confusion by God, like one vomiting from surfeit what he has taken in: because thy iniquity and its just punishment will overflow upon thee: as it is said in the Psalm, [[Ps 7:16|He hath opened a pit and dug it: and he is fallen into the hole he made.|Lacum aperuit, et effodit eum; et incidit in foveam quam fecit.]] and in the book of Proverbs too, [[Prov 11:6|the unjust shall be caught in their own snares|In insidiis suis capientur iniqui]]. And in Isaias we read: [[Is 3:11|Woe to the wicked unto evil: for the reward of his hands shall be given him.|Væ impio in malum; retributio manuum ejus fiet ei]] [[2:16|on thy glory|Super gloriam tuam]], that is, after the most empty boasting and frivolous exultation that thou hadst in supplanting others. This is said against those who rejoice in the ruin of others.

paras.t: Quia iniquitas Libani, id est impietas gloriæ sæcularis apparenter florentis: Libanus namque candidatio interpretatur; operiet te, id est, tuæ dejectionis atque miseriæ causa erit; et vastitas animalium deterrebit eos, id est, angustia quam impii rationalibus inferunt creaturis, erit causa quod et ipsi a Deo deterrebuntur in tempore ultionis.
paras.en: [[2:17|For the iniquity of Libanus|Quia iniquitas Libani]], that is, the wickedness of worldly glory, outwardly flourishing: for Libanus is interpreted “whitening” [*candidatio*; the name was taken from the Hebrew for “white”]; [[2:17|shall cover thee|operiet te]], that is, it will be the cause of thy downfall and misery; [[2:17|and the ravaging of beasts shall terrify them|et vastitas animalium deterrebit eos]], that is, the distress which the wicked inflict on rational creatures will be the cause why they themselves will be terrified by God in the time of vengeance.

paras.t: Quid prodest sculptile, quia sculpsit illud fictor suus? Hoc generaliter contra idololatras accipi potest: contra quos dicitur in Psalmo, Confundantur omnes qui adorant sculptilia, et qui gloriantur in simulacris suis; itemque in Deuteronomio, Maledictus omnis qui fecerit sculptile, et conflatile opus manuum artificum. Specialius vero accipitur contra omnes vitiosos, qui creaturæ potius quam Creatori inhærent, et aliquid sensualiter diligunt, cujus phantasmati tanquam idolo cuidam intenti sunt: quorum deus venter est, vel venus, aut certe pecunia, seu gloria mundi: quibus implendum est quod in fine primæ suæ Canonicæ scribit Joannes, Custodite vos a simulacris. Nil ergo inordinate amemus, sed Deus sit in nobis ratio diligendi omnia quæ præter eum amamus; nec vanis imaginibus cor nostrum depingamus, præsertim tempore divinorum, quatenus mente pura, nuda, indepicta et integra ei vacare possimus.
paras.en: [[2:18|What doth the graven thing avail, because the maker thereof hath graven it|Quid prodest sculptile, quia sculpsit illud fictor suus]]? This can be taken in general against idolaters, against whom it is said in the Psalm, [[Ps 96:7|Let them be all confounded that adore graven things, and that glory in their idols|Confundantur omnes qui adorant sculptilia, et qui gloriantur in simulacris suis]]; and likewise in Deuteronomy, [[Deut 27:15|Cursed be the man that maketh a graven and molten thing|Maledictus omnis qui fecerit sculptile, et conflatile]], [[Deut 27:15|the work of the hands of artificers|opus manuum artificum]]. But more particularly it is taken against all the vicious, who cleave to the creature rather than to the Creator, and love something with the senses, on whose image they are intent as on some idol: [[Phil 3:19|whose God is their belly|quorum deus venter est]], or lust [*venus*, a play on *venter*, “belly”], or else money, or the glory of the world: in whom must be fulfilled what John writes at the end of his first Canonical Epistle, [[1 John 5:21|keep yourselves from idols|Custodite vos a simulacris]]. Let us therefore love nothing inordinately, but let God be in us the reason for loving all the things that we love besides him; and let us not paint our heart with vain images, especially at the time of divine service, so that with a mind pure, bare, unpainted and whole we may be free for him.

paras.t: Dominus in templo sancto suo, id est triumphanti ac militanti Ecclesia, imo in omni mente devota et corpore devotorum, sicut Apostolus, Templum (inquit) Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos; et rursus, Corpora vestra templum sunt Spiritus Sancti. In Ecclesia militante est per gratiosam inhabitationem, in Ecclesia triumphanti per gloriosam manifestationem, ubique autem per essentiam, præsentiam atque potentiam, quia in ipso vivimus, movemur, et sumus. Nusquam vero est per inclusionem vel circumscriptionem. — Cetera innotescunt ex dictis in præcedenti articulo.
paras.en: [[2:20|the Lord is in his holy temple|Dominus in templo sancto suo]], that is, in the Church triumphant and militant, nay, in every devout mind and in the bodies of the devout, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 3:17|the temple of God is holy, which you are|Templum (inquit) Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos]]; and again, [[1 Cor 6:19|your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost|Corpora vestra templum sunt Spiritus Sancti]] [Denis reads *corpora*, “your bodies”]. He is in the Church militant by a dwelling of grace, in the Church triumphant by a manifestation of glory, but everywhere by essence, presence and power, because [[Acts 17:28|in him we live and move and are|in ipso vivimus, movemur, et sumus]]. But he is nowhere by being enclosed or circumscribed. The rest is clear from what was said in the preceding article.

3.title: Declaratio capituli tertii, scilicet cantici: Domine, audivi auditionem tuam, et timui.
3.title_en: Explanation of the third chapter, that is, of the canticle: O Lord, I have heard thy hearing, and was afraid.

paras.t: Præsenti capitulo præmittitur in Hebræo titulus iste: Oratio Habacuc prophetæ, pro ignorantiis, vel, ignorationibus, secundum Hieronymum. Estque sensus, secundum eumdem: Quia in principio hujus libri temere dixit Propheta: Usquequo, Domine, clamabo, et non exaudies? quare non respicis super inique agentes, et taces devorante impio justiorem se? propterea egreditur perversum judicium; et quædam similia, quæ prima facie non videntur bene sonare: nunc agit pœnitentiam, et plangit quod temere est locutus, et veniam deprecatur, eo quod contra divina judicia murmuravit, quia ignorans fecit.
paras.en: This chapter is headed in the Hebrew by this title: [[3:1|A PRAYER OF Habakkuk THE PROPHET FOR IGNORANCES|Oratio Habacuc prophetæ, pro ignorantiis]], or, *for ignorings*, according to Jerome. And the sense, according to the same Jerome, is this: because at the beginning of this book the Prophet said rashly: [[1:2|How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear?|Usquequo, Domine, clamabo, et non exaudies?]] [[1:13|Why lookest thou upon them that do unjust things, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself?|quare non respicis super inique agentes, et taces devorante impio justiorem se?]] [Denis reads "why dost thou not look upon"; the margin gives Hab. i, 2, then Ibid. 3, 13: the words are from 1:2 and 1:13], [[1:4|therefore wrong judgment goeth forth|propterea egreditur perversum judicium]], and some like things which at first sight do not seem to sound well: now he does penance, and laments that he spoke rashly, and begs pardon for having murmured against the divine judgments, because he did it in ignorance.

paras.t: Sed huic expositioni quidam objiciunt, quoniam verisimile non videtur quod Propheta divinitus illustratus, ignoraverit divina judicia esse justa saltem in generali, quamvis modum rectitudinis nescierit in particulari. Itaque dicunt, quod sicut in propria persona non dixit præinducta verba contra divinam justitiam, sed in persona infirmorum, ita nunc orat in persona eorum, ut et murmuratio et oratio in illorum persona prolata credatur. Istud apparet satis probabiliter dictum, et verba Hieronymi possunt ad idem reduci, præsertim quum ipse S. Hieronymus in exordio expositionis hujus prophetiæ testetur, Prophetam loqui verba præallegata in persona Judaicæ plebis. Et postea ait: Hæc dicit Propheta, non quod ipse sic sentiat, sed quod impatientiam humanam in sua persona exprimat, sicut frequenter apostolus Paulus varias in se hominum recipit personas exprimitque sententias. Unde quod nunc ait Hieronymus, Prophetam temere et ex ignorantia esse locutum, veniam quoque precari, accipi potest ita, ut ipsa temeritas et ignorantia quæ in verbis Prophetæ sonuerunt, referantur ad eos in quorum persona locutus est.
paras.en: But some raise this objection against this exposition: it does not seem likely that the Prophet, enlightened by God, did not know that the divine judgments are just, at least in general, even if he did not know the manner of their rightness in particular. And so they say that, just as he did not speak the words quoted above against the divine justice in his own person, but in the person of the weak, so now he prays in their person, so that both the murmuring and the prayer are to be taken as uttered in their person. This seems said with fair probability, and Jerome's words can be brought round to the same, especially since St. Jerome himself, at the opening of his exposition of this prophecy, testifies that the Prophet speaks the words quoted above in the person of the Jewish people. And afterwards he says: The Prophet says these things not because he himself thinks so, but because he expresses human impatience in his own person, as the apostle Paul often takes on himself the persons of various men and expresses their opinions. Hence what Jerome now says, that the Prophet spoke rashly and from ignorance, and also begs pardon, can be taken in such a way that the very rashness and ignorance which sounded in the Prophet's words are referred to those in whose person he spoke.

paras.t: Porro, si quis dicat, non oportere Prophetam a peccatis venialibus excusari, et ideo, licet agnoverat Deum esse justissimum, ac ejus judicia esse justa non dubitavit in generali, tamen ex interno cordis sui dolore rationem aliqualiter offuscante et impatientia quadam, orta ex populi Judæorum gravissima oppressione, temere sit locutus (sicut et Jonas propheta fugit a facie Domini; et non obstante quod Dominus dixit, Numquid bene irasceris tu? respondit, Bene irascor usque ad mortem; Job etiam profitetur: Insipienter locutus sum, et quæ ultra modum excederent scientiam meam; idcirco ipse me reprehendo, et ago pœnitentiam in favilla et cinere): si, inquam, quis dicat temere esse sanctum Habacuc in hac parte locutum, ex vehementi dolore rectum rationis judicium in particularibus aliqualiter impedientem, atque ob id veniam postulantem, responsionis hujus vigorem studiosis committo.
paras.en: Further, if anyone should say that the Prophet need not be excused from venial sins, and therefore that, although he acknowledged God to be most just and did not doubt that His judgments are just in general, yet, from the inward grief of his heart somewhat darkening his reason, and from a certain impatience arising from the most grievous oppression of the Jewish people, he spoke rashly (as the prophet Jonas too fled from the face of the Lord[[Jon 1:3||]]; and although the Lord said, [[Jon 4:9|Dost thou think thou hast reason to be angry|Numquid bene irasceris tu?]]? he answered, [[Jon 4:9|I am angry with reason even unto death|Bene irascor usque ad mortem]]; Job too confesses: [[Job 42:3|I have spoken unwisely, and things that above measure exceeded my knowledge|Insipienter locutus sum, et quæ ultra modum excederent scientiam meam]]; [[Job 42:6|Therefore I reprehend myself, and do penance in dust and ashes|idcirco ipse me reprehendo, et ago pœnitentiam in favilla et cinere]]): if, I say, anyone should say that holy Habacuc spoke rashly in this passage, his vehement grief somewhat hindering the right judgment of reason in particulars, and that for this reason he asks pardon, I leave the strength of this answer to the studious to weigh.

paras.t: Ait ergo beatus Propheta: Domine, audivi interiori auditu, te intus in anima per angelum tuum loquentem: quemadmodum Zacharias, Angelus (inquit) loquebatur in me. Vel certe etiam exteriori auditu per angelum. Certum est namque, angelum Dei visibiliter apparuisse, sensibiliterque foras locutum fuisse huic Prophetæ, quando in Babylonem tulit eumdem, quemadmodum in Daniele scribitur. Unde et ea quæ nunc scribit, extrinsecus forte audivit. Auditionem tuam, id est res auditu perceptas, videlicet dejectionem et pœnam regis Babylonis ac populi ejus, in præcedenti capitulo positas. Et timui te, considerando rigorem tuæ justitiæ, et quam horrendum sit incidere in manus Dei viventis. Denique Isaias quid sibi contigerat, quum Babyloniorum afflictiones sibi Deus præostendisset, pandit dicens: Propterea repleti sunt lumbi mei dolore; corrui quum audirem, conturbatus sum quum viderem, emarcuit cor meum.
paras.en: The blessed Prophet therefore says: [[3:2|O Lord, I have heard|Domine, audivi]] with the inward hearing, thee speaking within, in my soul, through thy angel: as Zacharias says, [[Zach 1:9|the angel|Angelus]] (he says) [[Zach 1:9|that spoke in me|loquebatur in me]]. Or else also with the outward hearing, through an angel. For it is certain that an angel of God appeared visibly to this Prophet and spoke to him outwardly, to the senses, when he carried him to Babylon, as is written in Daniel[[Dan 14:35||]]. Hence he may perhaps also have heard from without the things he now writes. [[3:2|thy hearing|Auditionem tuam]], that is, the things perceived by hearing, namely the overthrow and punishment of the king of Babylon and of his people, set down in the preceding chapter[[2:6||]]. [[3:2|and was afraid|Et timui]] of thee, considering the rigour of thy justice, and that [[Heb 10:31|It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God|horrendum sit incidere in manus Dei viventis]]. Lastly, Isaias makes known what had happened to him when God had shown him beforehand the afflictions of the Babylonians, saying: [[Is 21:3|Therefore are my loins filled with pain|Propterea repleti sunt lumbi mei dolore]]; [[Is 21:3|I fell down at the hearing of it, I was troubled at the seeing of it|corrui quum audirem, conturbatus sum quum viderem]], [[Is 21:4|My heart failed|Emarcuit cor meum]].

paras.t: Domine, opus tuum est præinducta punitio Chaldæorum, quoniam tua virtute potius quam humana potestate peracta est; in medio annorum, id est in virili ætate ipsius Balthasar regis Babylonis, vivifica illud, id est, ad effectum perduc præfatam Chaldæorum seu Babyloniorum dejectionem. Balthasar quippe fuit filius filii Nabuchodonosor regis Babylonis: cujus Balthasar tempore, Medi ac Persæ demoliti sunt Babylonem. Et quoniam ætas virilis est medium vitæ humanæ, ipse Balthasar, qui in virili ætate occisus est juvenis, in medio annorum fertur occisus. Juxta quem modum loquitur Ezechias: Ego dixi, In dimidio dierum meorum vadam ad portas inferi, id est, ad limbum patrum descendam. Auditis enim sermonibus Isaiæ, putavit se in virili ætate ac juventute mox moriturum. — Vel sic et fructuosius: Domine, opus tuum est quod supra dixisti: Apparebit in finem, et non mentietur; si moram fecerit, exspecta illum, quia veniens veniet, etc.: id est, incarnatio et missio Christi in mundum, est, o Deus Pater, vel, Deus Trinitas, opus tuum præcipuum; in medio annorum, id est in plenitudine temporum, seu tempore gratiæ, quod inter annum iræ et annum gloriæ medium est, vivifica illud, Christum actualiter mittendo in mundum ad liberandum genus humanum.
paras.en: [[3:2|O Lord, thy work|Domine, opus tuum]] is the punishment of the Chaldeans spoken of above, since it was accomplished by thy power rather than by human might; [[3:2|in the midst of the years|in medio annorum]], that is, in the manhood of Balthasar himself, king of Babylon, [[3:2|bring it to life|vivifica illud]], that is, bring to effect the aforesaid overthrow of the Chaldeans or Babylonians. For Balthasar was the son of the son of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon; and in the time of this Balthasar the Medes and Persians destroyed Babylon[[Dan 5:30||]][[Dan 5:31||]]. And since manhood is the middle of human life, Balthasar, who was slain as a young man in his manhood, is said to have been slain in the midst of his years. In the same way Ezechias speaks: [[Is 38:10|I said: In the midst of my days I shall go to the gates of hell|Ego dixi, In dimidio dierum meorum vadam ad portas inferi]], that is, I shall go down to the limbo of the fathers. For when he had heard the words of Isaias, he thought he was soon to die in his manhood and youth. — Or thus, and more fruitfully: [[3:2|O Lord, thy work|Domine, opus tuum]] is what thou saidst above: [[2:3|it shall appear at the end, and shall not lie: if it make any delay, wait for it: for it shall surely come|Apparebit in finem, et non mentietur; si moram fecerit, exspecta illum, quia veniens veniet]], etc.: that is, the incarnation and the sending of Christ into the world is, O God the Father, or, O God the Trinity, thy chief work; [[3:2|in the midst of the years|in medio annorum]], that is, in the fulness of times[[Gal 4:4||]], or in the time of grace, which is midway between the year of wrath and the year of glory, [[3:2|bring it to life|vivifica illud]], by actually sending Christ into the world to set mankind free.

paras.t: Consequenter Propheta ostendit, se certificatum a Deo de adimpletione et verificatione eorum quæ jam postulavit. In medio annorum: de quibus jam dictum est; notum facies, id est, opere demonstrabis vera esse quæ dixi, videlicet Chaldæorum punitionem seu Christi adventum. Quum iratus fueris generi humano propter originale peccatum, januam gloriæ clausam tenendo, et nullum Sanctorum ad regnum cœlorum admittendo, misericordiæ recordaberis, Unigenitum tuum ad hominum redemptionem, o Pater piissime, destinando: sicut Apostolus ait, Quum venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum in mundum; itemque Joannes, In hoc apparuit caritas Dei, quoniam unigenitum Filium suum misit in mundum. Vel sic: Quum iratus fueris, misericordiæ recordaberis: id est, postquam Chaldæos juste dejeceris, populum Judæorum clementer de captivitate Babylonica liberabis per Cyrum regem Persarum, prout Isaias prædixit, et tempore Esdræ impletum est. Potest quoque ita exponi: Quum iratus fueris, vel Chaldæis, vel generi humano, misericordiæ recordaberis, citra condignum puniendo, et justæ ultioni misericordem relaxationem miscendo: quemadmodum ait Psalmista, Universæ viæ Domini misericordia et veritas. Ideo idem ait Psalmista: Aut obliviscetur misereri Deus? aut continebit in ira sua misericordias suas? Absit autem ut hæc ita intelligantur, quasi tandem finienda sint supplicia damnatorum, ut opinati sunt quidam. Denique nec ita intelligenda sunt hæc, quasi in Deum cadat ira sive oblivio vel recordatio proprie dicta secundum veritatem, sed per similitudinem quamdam, quantum ad operationem extrinsecam: ut iratus dicatur, quando ad modum irati rigorose ulciscitur; et oblivisci, dum misereri vel suffragari desistit; recordari quoque, dum quasi de novo quid operatur. Sic equidem ait Psalmista: Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris me in finem? et, Exsurge, quare obdormis, Domine?
paras.en: Next the Prophet shows that he has been assured by God of the fulfilment and making true of the things he has just asked for. [[3:2|In the midst of the years|In medio annorum]], of which we have just spoken, [[3:2|thou shalt make it known|notum facies]], that is, thou wilt show by deed that what I have said is true, namely the punishment of the Chaldeans, or the coming of Christ. [[3:2|when thou art angry|Quum iratus fueris]] with mankind because of original sin, keeping the gate of glory shut and admitting none of the Saints to the kingdom of heaven, [[3:2|thou wilt remember mercy|misericordiæ recordaberis]], appointing thy Only-begotten, O most loving Father, for the redemption of men: as the Apostle says, [[Gal 4:4|when the fulness of the time was come, God sent his Son|Quum venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum]] into the world; and likewise John: [[1 John 4:9|By this hath the charity of God appeared|In hoc apparuit caritas Dei]] [[1 John 4:9|because God hath sent his only begotten Son into the world|quoniam unigenitum Filium suum misit in mundum]]. Or thus: [[3:2|when thou art angry|Quum iratus fueris]], [[3:2|thou wilt remember mercy|misericordiæ recordaberis]]: that is, after thou hast justly overthrown the Chaldeans, thou wilt mercifully set the Jewish people free from the Babylonian captivity through Cyrus king of the Persians, as Isaias foretold[[Is 45:1||]], and as was fulfilled in the time of Esdras[[1 Esd 1:1||]]. It can also be expounded thus: [[3:2|when thou art angry|Quum iratus fueris]], either with the Chaldeans or with mankind, [[3:2|thou wilt remember mercy|misericordiæ recordaberis]], punishing short of what is deserved, and mingling a merciful easing with just vengeance: as the Psalmist says, [[Ps 24:10|All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth|Universæ viæ Domini misericordia et veritas]]. Therefore the same Psalmist says: [[Ps 76:10|Or will God forget to shew mercy? or will he in his anger shut up his mercies?|Aut obliviscetur misereri Deus? aut continebit in ira sua misericordias suas?]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxvi, 10; the words are Ps 76:10]. But far be it that these words should be understood as though the punishments of the damned were at length to come to an end, as some have held. Nor again are they to be understood as though anger, or forgetting, or remembering, properly so called, fell on God in truth, but by a certain likeness, as to his outward working: so that he is said to be angry when he takes vengeance rigorously, after the manner of one who is angry; to forget, when he ceases to have mercy or to help; and to remember, when he works something as it were anew. So indeed the Psalmist says: [[Ps 12:1|How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me unto the end?|Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris me in finem?]] and, [[Ps 43:23|Arise, why sleepest thou, O Lord?|Exsurge, quare obdormis, Domine?]]

paras.t: Deus ab austro veniet. Hoc ita exponit S. Hieronymus: A meridie, a claro lumine, a filiis lucis veniet Deus, ad quem Sponsa ait in Canticis: Ubi pascis, ubi cubas in meridie? Deus etenim semper in meridie est, puta in claritate patriæ et lumine gloriæ; et inde venire asseritur, non quod localiter moveatur, sed quod agnitio ejus inde descendat ad nos, secundum quod ait Psalmista: Inclina cœlos tuos, et descende. Et Sanctus de monte Pharan, id est, Christus Sanctus Sanctorum veniet in hunc mundum de sublimi solio Patris æterni. Pharan namque interpretatur, os videntis. Est autem os quoddam intellectuale internum, quo verbum mentale profertur: de quo loquitur Isaias, Os Domini non interrogastis; et rursus, Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum. Pater ergo æternus est mons Pharan, id est altissima mens, omnia cernens, et omnem visionem fontaliter causans. De quo Filius prodit, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam.
paras.en: [[3:3|God will come from the south|Deus ab austro veniet]]. St. Jerome expounds this thus: From the midday, from the bright light, from the children of light God will come, to whom the Bride says in the Canticle: [[Cant 1:6|where thou feedest, where thou liest in the midday|Ubi pascis, ubi cubas in meridie?]]? For God is always in the midday, that is, in the brightness of the heavenly fatherland and the light of glory; and he is said to come from there, not because he moves from place to place, but because the knowledge of him comes down from there to us, according to what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 143:5|bow down thy heavens and descend|Inclina cœlos tuos, et descende]]. [[3:3|and the holy one from mount Pharan|Et Sanctus de monte Pharan]], that is, Christ, the Holy of Holies, will come into this world from the lofty throne of the eternal Father. For *Pharan* is interpreted "the mouth of one seeing". Now there is a certain inward, intellectual mouth, by which the word of the mind is uttered; of which Isaias speaks: [[Is 30:2|have not asked at my mouth|Os Domini non interrogastis]] [Denis reads "ye have not asked at the mouth of the Lord"]; and again: [[Is 45:23|the word of justice shall go out of my mouth|Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum]]. The eternal Father, then, is mount Pharan, that is, the highest mind, seeing all things and the fountain-cause of all vision. From him the Son comes forth, according to that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 24:5|I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures|Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam]].

paras.t: Quidam vel litteralius vel grossius ita exponunt: Deus ab austro veniet: id est, quemadmodum Deus venit a plaga australi, quando perduxit filios Israel ad terram promissionis ab Ægypto, quæ est ad austrum quoad Judæam; sic veniet cum Medis ac Persis ad redimendum eos de captivitate Babylonica. Et Sanctus de monte Pharan: id est, sicut deduxit filios Israel per locum illum deserti, ita reducet eos de Babylone. — Sed hac expositione gratiosior mihi apparet, quam Hieronymus asserit se a quodam audisse Hebræo: qui dixit, quod Bethlehem, in qua natus est Christus Deus, sit sita ad austrum: ideo eo quod ait Propheta, Deus ab austro veniet, designatur, quod in Bethlehem nasceretur, et inde consurgeret Christus; et Sanctus de monte Pharan, id est, Salvator qui legem dedit in monte Sinai, juxta quem Pharan est locus vicinus, ipse est Deus ab austro adveniens. Huic versiculo addit Hieronymus adverbium, Semper, quod (ut ait) etiam in Hebræo habetur: quo designatur, quod Salvator in universis beneficiis suis præteritis, præsentibus ac futuris, sit unus auctor, idemque legislator. De quo ad Hebræos testatur Apostolus: Jesus Christus heri et hodie, ipse et in sæcula. Postremo, istum Hebræum de quo expositionem hanc suscepit Hieronymus, puto ad fidem fuisse conversum. Judæi namque in Judaismo manentes, non dicunt Messiam futurum verum Deum, sed hominem purum.
paras.en: Some expound it, either more literally or more crudely, thus: [[3:3|God will come from the south|Deus ab austro veniet]]: that is, as God came from the southern quarter when he brought the children of Israel to the land of promise out of Egypt, which lies to the south of Judea, so he will come with the Medes and Persians to redeem them from the Babylonian captivity. [[3:3|and the holy one from mount Pharan|Et Sanctus de monte Pharan]]: that is, as he led the children of Israel through that place of the desert[[Num 10:12||]], so he will lead them back from Babylon. — But more pleasing to me than this exposition is the one which Jerome says he heard from a certain Hebrew, who said that Bethlehem, in which Christ God was born, lies to the south; and so by the Prophet's saying, [[3:3|God will come from the south|Deus ab austro veniet]], it is signified that Christ would be born in Bethlehem and rise up from there; and [[3:3|the holy one from mount Pharan|Sanctus de monte Pharan]], that is, the Saviour, who gave the law on mount Sinai, near which Pharan is a neighbouring place[[Deut 33:2||]], is himself God coming from the south. To this verse Jerome adds the adverb *Always*, which (as he says) is also found in the Hebrew: by which it is signified that the Saviour, in all his benefits, past, present and to come, is the one author and the same lawgiver. Of whom the Apostle testifies to the Hebrews: [[Heb 13:8|Jesus Christ, yesterday, and today: and the same for ever|Jesus Christus heri et hodie, ipse et in sæcula]]. Lastly, I think that this Hebrew from whom Jerome took this exposition had been converted to the faith. For the Jews who remain in Judaism do not say that the Messias to come is true God, but a mere man.

paras.t: Operuit cœlos gloria ejus: id est, divina majestas, quæ vere immensa est, omnes orbes cœlestes et beatos cœli empyrei cives tegit, ambit, circumdat, imo implet ac penetrat; nec tamen includitur neque finitur. Hinc in Ecclesiastico increata Sapientia contestatur: Gyrum cœli circuivi sola, et profundum abyssi penetravi. Vel dicitur gloria Dei (id est clara ejus notitia, gloriosus effectus, seu cognitio excellentiæ ejus) operire cœlos, id est Beatos, et eos quoque quorum conversatio est in cœlis: quoniam lumen gloriæ, splendor gratiæ, claritas sapientiæ exuberanter super eos descendit, et spiritualiter tegit eos ac implet, juxta illud Job: Numquid est numerus militum ejus? et super quem non surgit lumen ipsius? Juxta hunc sensum scriptum est in libro Sapientiæ: Dextera sua teget eos. Et laudis ejus plena est terra, id est Ecclesia militans per orbem terræ diffusa: quemadmodum cantamus in Psalmo, A solis ortu usque ad occasum laudabile nomen Domini; et item, Domine Dominus noster, quam admirabile est nomen tuum in universa terra! Hinc Isaias: Repleta, inquit, est terra scientia Domini; rursusque, A finibus terræ audivimus laudes, gloriam Justi. Denique in eodem Isaia, Seraphim clamant: Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, Dominus Deus exercituum; plena est omnis terra gloria ejus. Unde per Jeremiam Dominus loquitur: Omnes cognoscent me a minimo eorum usque ad maximum, scilicet tempore gratiæ.
paras.en: [[3:3|His glory covered the heavens|Operuit cœlos gloria ejus]]: that is, the divine majesty, which is truly immeasurable, covers, encompasses, surrounds, nay fills and pervades all the heavenly spheres and the blessed citizens of the empyrean heaven; and yet it is not enclosed or bounded. Hence in Ecclesiasticus the uncreated Wisdom bears witness: [[Ecclus 24:8|I alone have compassed the circuit of heaven, and have penetrated into the bottom of the deep|Gyrum cœli circuivi sola, et profundum abyssi penetravi]]. Or the glory of God (that is, the clear knowledge of him, his glorious working, or the knowledge of his excellence) is said to cover the heavens, that is, the Blessed, and those also whose [[Phil 3:20|conversation is in heaven|conversatio est in cœlis]]: since the light of glory, the splendour of grace, the brightness of wisdom comes down abundantly upon them, and spiritually covers and fills them, according to that word of Job: [[Job 25:3|Is there any numbering of his soldiers? and upon whom shall not his light arise?|Numquid est numerus militum ejus? et super quem non surgit lumen ipsius?]] In this sense it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:17|with his right hand he will cover them|Dextera sua teget eos]]. [[3:3|and the earth is full of his praise|Et laudis ejus plena est terra]], that is, the Church militant spread through the whole world: as we sing in the Psalm, [[Ps 112:3|From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise|A solis ortu usque ad occasum laudabile nomen Domini]]; and again, [[Ps 8:2|O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is thy name in the whole earth!|Domine Dominus noster, quam admirabile est nomen tuum in universa terra!]] Hence Isaias: [[Is 11:9|the earth is filled|Repleta]], he says, [[Is 11:9|with the knowledge of the Lord|est terra scientia Domini]]; and again: [[Is 24:16|From the ends of the earth we have heard praises, the glory of the just one|A finibus terræ audivimus laudes, gloriam Justi]]. Lastly, in the same Isaias the Seraphim[[Is 6:2||]] cry: [[Is 6:3|Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory|Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, Dominus Deus exercituum; plena est omnis terra gloria ejus]]. Hence the Lord speaks through Jeremias: [[Jer 31:34|all shall know me from the least of them even to the greatest|Omnes cognoscent me a minimo eorum usque ad maximum]], namely in the time of grace.

paras.t: Splendor ejus, id est unigenitus Filius Patris, qui (teste Apostolo) est splendor gloriæ et figura substantiæ Patris: est enim candor lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis, et imago bonitatis ejus; ut lux erit, id est, hominibus clare innotescet, et Patri esse æqualis noscetur, ita quod erit in mente fidelium sicut lux Patris seu Pater, a quo generatur: quemadmodum de ipso ait Joannes, Erat lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem. Quod maxime factum constat per Apostolorum prædicationem, post Christi passionem. Unde pro hac sua clarificatione Christus passioni jam proximus deprecatus est, dicens: Clarifica me tu, Pater, apud temetipsum, claritate quam habui antequam mundus fieret.
paras.en: [[3:4|His brightness|Splendor ejus]], that is, the only-begotten Son of the Father, who (as the Apostle witnesses) is [[Heb 1:3|the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance|splendor gloriæ et figura substantiæ]] [Denis: "of the Father's substance"]: for he is [[Wis 7:26|the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of God's majesty, and the image of his goodness|candor lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis, et imago bonitatis ejus]]; [[3:4|shall be as the light|ut lux erit]], that is, he will become clearly known to men, and will be known to be equal to the Father, so that in the minds of the faithful he will be as the light of the Father, or as the Father, from whom he is begotten: as John says of him, [[John 1:9|That was the true light, which enlighteneth every man|Erat lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem]]. And this, it is clear, came about above all through the preaching of the Apostles after Christ's passion. Hence for this glorifying of his, Christ, when his passion was now near, prayed, saying: [[John 17:5|glorify thou me, O Father, with thyself, with the glory which I had, before the world was|Clarifica me tu, Pater, apud temetipsum, claritate quam habui antequam mundus fieret]].

paras.t: Cornua in manibus ejus. Secundum Hieronymum, per cornua intelliguntur regna, sicut in Daniele decem cornua decem regna vocantur. Et in libro primo Regum, quo dicitur, Exaltabit cornu Christi sui, per cornu designatur regia dignitas Salvatoris. Est itaque sensus, quod in potestate et manu Christi sint omnia regna: ipse enim est Rex regum et Dominus dominantium, cui data est omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra. De quo in Daniele legitur: Adspiciebam in visione noctis, et ecce in nubibus cœli quasi Filius hominis veniebat, et usque ad Antiquum dierum pervenit; et dedit ei potestatem, honorem et regnum; et omnes populi, tribus et linguæ servient ei. Possunt quoque per cornua intelligi capita clavorum Christi manibus infixorum, vel crucis extrema. Et quamvis manus Christi erant potius in cornibus crucis quam e converso, nihilo minus dicitur nunc, Cornua in manibus ejus, ad insinuandum quod crux fuit in manu seu potestate Christi, qui ait: Nemo tollit animam meam a me, sed ego ponam eam. Oblatus est enim, quia voluit. Nec dubium quin Christus rex Israel, Dei electus, poterat de cruce descendere, quando perditionis filii illud pro signo quærebant.
paras.en: [[3:4|horns are in his hands|Cornua in manibus ejus]]. According to Jerome, by horns are understood kingdoms, as in Daniel ten horns are called ten kingdoms[[Dan 7:7||]][[Dan 7:24||]]. And in the first book of Kings, where it is said, [[1 Kings 2:10|shall exalt the horn of his Christ|Exaltabit cornu Christi sui]], the royal dignity of the Saviour is signified by the horn. So the sense is that all kingdoms are in the power and hand of Christ: for he is [[Apoc 19:16|KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS|Rex regum et Dominus dominantium]], to whom [[Matt 28:18|All power is given|data est omnis potestas]] [[Matt 28:18|in heaven and in earth|in cœlo et in terra]]. Of whom we read in Daniel: [[Dan 7:13|I beheld, therefore, in the vision of the night, and lo, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and he came even to the ancient of days|Adspiciebam in visione noctis, et ecce in nubibus cœli quasi Filius hominis veniebat, et usque ad Antiquum dierum pervenit]]; [[Dan 7:14|he gave him power, and glory, and a kingdom: and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him|dedit ei potestatem, honorem et regnum; et omnes populi, tribus et linguæ servient ei]]. By the horns may also be understood the heads of the nails driven into Christ's hands, or the ends of the cross. And though Christ's hands were rather on the horns of the cross than the other way round, it is nevertheless said here, [[3:4|horns are in his hands|Cornua in manibus ejus]], to suggest that the cross was in the hand or power of Christ, who says: [[John 10:18|No man taketh it away from me: but I lay it down|Nemo tollit animam meam a me, sed ego ponam eam]] [Denis reads "No man taketh my life from me"]. For [[Is 53:7|He was offered because it was his own will|Oblatus est enim, quia voluit]]. Nor is there any doubt that Christ, the king of Israel[[Matt 27:42||]], the elect of God[[Luke 23:35||]], could have come down from the cross, when the sons of perdition were asking for that as a sign [the margin gives Matt. xxvii, 39–43; Luke xxiii, 35].

paras.t: Ibi abscondita est fortitudo ejus: quia in passione latuit omnipotentia Salvatoris, quemadmodum Isaias prædixit: Vidimus eum, et non erat adspectus, et quasi absconditus vultus ejus et despectus; et item, Inglorius erit inter viros adspectus ejus. Propter quod ait Christus in Psalmo: Ego autem sum vermis, et non homo; opprobrium hominum et abjectio plebis.
paras.en: [[3:4|There is his strength hid|Ibi abscondita est fortitudo ejus]]: because in the passion the almighty power of the Saviour lay hidden, as Isaias foretold: [[Is 53:2|we have seen him, and there was no sightliness|Vidimus eum, et non erat adspectus]], [[Is 53:3|and his look was as it were hidden and despised|et quasi absconditus vultus ejus et despectus]]; and again: [[Is 52:14|so shall his visage be inglorious among men|Inglorius erit inter viros adspectus ejus]]. For this reason Christ says in the Psalm: [[Ps 21:7|But I am a worm, and no man: the reproach of men, and the outcast of the people.|Ego autem sum vermis, et non homo; opprobrium hominum et abjectio plebis]]

paras.t: Ante faciem ejus ibit mors, id est, a facie Christi mors fugiet. Christus enim mortem expulit et occidit, sicut ait Apostolus: Absorpta est mors in victoria. Et in Osee ait Salvator: De morte redimam eos; ero mors tua, o mors! Siquidem Christus sua morte immortalitatem nobis perfectam promeruit, quam in resurrectione futura adipiscemur, atque a morte peccati nos liberavit. Hinc in Isaia asseritur: Præcipitabit Dominus mortem in sempiternum. Unde in Evangelio loquitur Christus: Qui credit in me, mortem non gustabit in æternum.
paras.en: [[3:5|Death shall go before his face|Ante faciem ejus ibit mors]], that is, death shall flee from the face of Christ. For Christ drove out death and slew it, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 15:54|Death is swallowed up in victory|Absorpta est mors in victoria]]. And in Osee the Saviour says: [[Osee 13:14|I will redeem them from death|De morte redimam eos]]; [[Osee 13:14|O death, I will be thy death|ero mors tua, o mors]]! For Christ by his death merited for us perfect immortality, which we shall gain in the resurrection to come, and he set us free from the death of sin. Hence it is declared in Isaias: the Lord [[Is 25:8|shall cast death down headlong for ever|Præcipitabit Dominus mortem in sempiternum]]. Hence in the Gospel Christ says: He that [[John 11:26|believeth in me|credit in me]] [[John 8:52|shall not taste death for ever|mortem non gustabit in æternum]] [Denis joins John 11:26 and John 8:52].

paras.t: Egredietur diabolus ante pedes ejus. Secundum Hieronymum sensus est, quod Christo de aqua baptismatis exeunti atque desertum intranti, mox occurrit diabolus tentans eum, prout apud Matthæum recolitur: Ductus est Jesus in desertum, ut tentaretur a diabolo. Hieronymus quoque affirmat hoc loco, quod coluber antiquus quadraginta diebus tentavit Jesum in solitudine. Vel sensus est, quod per Christi adventum, prædicationem et occisionem, victus atque fugatus est Satanas, ut in Joanne ait Salvator: Nunc princeps hujus mundi ejicietur foras. In hoc quippe apparuit Filius Dei, ut dissolvat opera diaboli. Denique in Evangeliis copiose narratur quemadmodum ab obsessis fugaverit Christus dæmonia, ita ut eo jam propinquante, timore diffugerent, juxta illud: Exibant dæmonia multa clamantia et dicentia: Quia tu es Filius Dei; et item: Jesu, Fili Dei summi, quid venisti ante tempus torquere nos?
paras.en: [[3:5|the devil shall go forth before his feet|Egredietur diabolus ante pedes ejus]]. According to Jerome the sense is that as Christ came out of the water of baptism and went into the desert, the devil at once met him and tempted him, as is recounted in Matthew: [[Matt 4:1|Jesus was led|Ductus est Jesus]] [[Matt 4:1|into the desert, to be tempted by the devil|in desertum, ut tentaretur a diabolo]]. Jerome also affirms in this place that the old serpent tempted Jesus in the wilderness for forty days. Or the sense is that through Christ's coming, preaching and death Satan was conquered and put to flight, as the Saviour says in John: [[John 12:31|now shall the prince of this world be cast out|Nunc princeps hujus mundi ejicietur foras]]. [[1 John 3:8|For this purpose|In hoc]] indeed [[1 John 3:8|the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil|apparuit Filius Dei, ut dissolvat opera diaboli]]. Lastly, it is told at length in the Gospels how Christ drove the devils out of the possessed, so that as soon as he drew near they fled away in fear, according to that word: [[Luke 4:41|devils went out from many, crying out and saying: Thou art the son of God|Exibant dæmonia multa clamantia et dicentia: Quia tu es Filius Dei]] [Denis reads "many devils went out"]; and again: [[Mark 5:7|Jesus the Son of the most high God|Jesu, Fili Dei summi]], why [[Matt 8:29|art thou come hither to torment us before the time?|venisti ante tempus torquere nos?]] [Denis joins Mark 5:7 (or Luke 8:28) and Matt 8:29]

paras.t: Stetit ipse Dominus, id est, in solio suæ majestatis quievit, et mensus est terram: quemadmodum ad Job testatur: Quis posuit mensuras terræ? aut quis tetendit super eam lineam? Et in Ecclesiastico: Altitudinem cœli, et latitudinem terræ, et profundum abyssi quis dimensus est? Ipse equidem in numero, pondere et mensura constituit universa. Vel, Mensus est terram, mittendo angelos per omnem orbem terrarum, secundum illud Zachariæ: Isti sunt quos misit Dominus, ut perambulent terram. Nam diabolus profitetur ad Dominum in libro Job: Circuivi terram et perambulavi eam. Vel, Mensus est terram, id est habitantes in terra, omnium personas, qualitates, gesta et merita considerando, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Oculi Domini multo lucidiores super solem, circumspicientes omnes vias hominum. Mensus est etiam homines, numerum eorum in se ipso æternaliter prædeterminando.
paras.en: [[3:6|He stood|Stetit]], the Lord himself, that is, he rested on the throne of his majesty, [[3:6|and measured the earth|et mensus est terram]]: as he testifies to Job: [[Job 38:5|Who hath laid the measures thereof|Quis posuit mensuras terræ?]]? [[Job 38:5|or who hath stretched the line upon it|aut quis tetendit super eam lineam?]]? [Denis reads "the measures of the earth"] And in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 1:2|Who hath measured the height of heaven, and the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss?|Altitudinem cœli, et latitudinem terræ, et profundum abyssi quis dimensus est?]] He indeed has established all things in number, weight and measure. Or, [[3:6|measured the earth|Mensus est terram]] by sending angels through the whole world, according to that word of Zacharias: [[Zach 1:10|These are they, whom the Lord hath sent to walk through the earth|Isti sunt quos misit Dominus, ut perambulent terram]]. For the devil confesses to the Lord in the book of Job: [[Job 1:7|I have gone round about the earth, and walked through it|Circuivi terram et perambulavi eam]]. Or, [[3:6|measured the earth|Mensus est terram]], that is, those who dwell on the earth, considering the persons, qualities, deeds and merits of all, according to that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 23:28|the eyes of the Lord are far brighter than the sun, beholding round about all the ways of men|Oculi Domini multo lucidiores super solem, circumspicientes omnes vias hominum]]. He also measured men by fixing their number beforehand in himself from eternity.

paras.t: Adspexit oculo æquitatis, et dissolvit gentes, impios atque incredulos subvertendo; et contriti sunt montes sæculi, id est majores elatioresque principes terræ. Fortioribus namque fortior instat cruciatus, et potentes potenter tormenta patientur, ut dicit Sapiens. Hinc scriptum est in Baruch: Ubi sunt principes gentium, qui dominantur super bestias terræ, qui in avibus cœli ludunt? Exterminati sunt, et ad inferos descenderunt. Incurvati sunt colles mundi, id est, principes minores humiliati sunt, ab itineribus æternitatis ejus, id est ab operibus seu processibus divinæ justitiæ, seu Dei æterni, ab æterno prævisis et præordinatis. Itinera itaque Dei possunt intelligi dispositiones rerum fiendarum in mente divina, secundum illud quod increata Sapientia loquitur, Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio; vel ipsi processus operum divinæ sapientiæ, pietatis, vel æquitatis, de quibus Salomon fassus est, Viæ ejus, viæ pulchræ. De hac montium colliumque justa depressione scriptum est in Isaia: Dominus Deus exercituum cogitavit hoc, ut detraheret superbiam omnis gloriæ, et ad ignominiam deduceret universos inclytos terræ; et alio loco, Incurvabitur sublimitas hominum, et humiliabitur altitudo virorum.
paras.en: [[3:6|He beheld|Adspexit]] with the eye of equity, [[3:6|and melted the nations|et dissolvit gentes]], overthrowing the ungodly and unbelieving; [[3:6|and the ancient mountains were crushed to pieces|et contriti sunt montes sæculi]], that is, the greater and prouder princes of the earth. For [[Wis 6:9|a greater punishment is ready for the more mighty|Fortioribus namque fortior instat cruciatus]], and [[Wis 6:7|the mighty shall be mightily tormented|potentes potenter tormenta patientur]], as the Wise Man says. Hence it is written in Baruch: [[Bar 3:16|Where are the princes of the nations, and they that rule over the beasts that are upon the earth?|Ubi sunt principes gentium, qui dominantur super bestias terræ]] [[Bar 3:17|That take their diversion with the birds of the air|qui in avibus cœli ludunt?]]? [[Bar 3:19|They are cut off, and are gone down to hell|Exterminati sunt, et ad inferos descenderunt]]. [[3:6|The hills of the world were bowed down|Incurvati sunt colles mundi]], that is, the lesser princes were humbled, [[3:6|by the journeys of his eternity|ab itineribus æternitatis ejus]], that is, by the works or proceedings of the divine justice, or of the eternal God, foreseen and foreordained from eternity. And so the journeys of God may be understood as the plans, in the divine mind, of things to be done, according to what the uncreated Wisdom says: [[Prov 8:22|The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made any thing from the beginning|Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio]]; or as the very proceedings of the works of the divine wisdom, mercy or equity, of which Solomon declared: [[Prov 3:17|Her ways are beautiful ways|Viæ ejus, viæ pulchræ]] [Denis takes them as "his ways", the ways of God]. Of this just bringing down of the mountains and hills it is written in Isaias: [[Is 23:9|The Lord of hosts hath designed it, to pull down the pride of all glory, and bring to disgrace all the glorious ones of the earth|Dominus Deus exercituum cogitavit hoc, ut detraheret superbiam omnis gloriæ, et ad ignominiam deduceret universos inclytos terræ]]; and in another place: [[Is 2:17|the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be humbled|Incurvabitur sublimitas hominum, et humiliabitur altitudo virorum]].

paras.t: Potest quoque exponi in bono, ut Deus dicatur oculo suæ clementiæ gentes adspexisse, et dissolvisse corda eorum ad pœnitentiam. Sicque, contriti sunt montes, non ipsis, sed eorum elatione ac vitiis demolitis, juxta quod scriptum est, Verte impios, et non erunt; et incurvati sunt colles mundi salubriter ad veram ac humilem pristinæ animositatis depressionem. De hujuscemodi optima incurvatione legitur in Baruch: Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali et incedit curva, dat gloriam Domino. Quidam referunt præinducta specialiter ad Chaldæos, a Persis ac Medis divina præordinatione subversos.
paras.en: It can also be expounded in a good sense: God is said to have beheld the nations with the eye of his mercy, and to have melted their hearts unto penance. And so [[3:6|the ancient mountains were crushed to pieces|contriti sunt montes]], not they themselves, but their pride and vices being pulled down, according to what is written: [[Prov 12:7|Turn the wicked, and they shall not be|Verte impios, et non erunt]]; and [[3:6|the hills of the world were bowed down|incurvati sunt colles mundi]], to their health, unto a true and humble lowering of their former haughtiness. Of this best kind of bowing down we read in Baruch: [[Bar 2:18|the soul that is sorrowful for the greatness of evil she hath done, and goeth bowed down|Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali et incedit curva]], [[Bar 2:18|giveth glory|dat gloriam]] to the Lord. Some refer what has been said specially to the Chaldeans, overthrown by the Persians and Medes by the divine foreordaining.

paras.t: Pro iniquitate vidi tentoria Æthiopiæ: id est, iniquitatum suarum demeritis fiunt homines spiritualiter denigrati atque dæmonibus assimilati, imo et tabernacula dæmonum, sicut electi sunt domus et templum Dei. Turbabuntur pelles terræ Madian. Septuaginta transtulerunt, Pavebunt tabernacula terræ Madian. Unde secundum Hieronymum, eosdem debemus accipere tabernacula Æthiopum et Madianitarum: qui pro suis peccatis turbabuntur timore horribili, quum se viderint condemnandos. Spiritualiter, pelles Madian, intelliguntur propriæ voluntates, passiones animæ et concupiscentiæ carnis, quibus se tegunt, armant, et induunt vitiosi, rebelles, et inobedientes. Quidam exponunt ista ad litteram, ita quod pro iniquitate destructionis templi Jerusalem, tentoria Æthiopiæ et Madian sint turbata, id est a Persis et Medis debellata: quoniam Æthiopes et Madianitæ fuerunt, ut dicunt, cum rege Babylonis in destructione templi, et postea cum Babyloniis interfecti: quod unde probari possit, ignoro.
paras.en: [[3:7|I saw the tents of Ethiopia for their iniquity|Pro iniquitate vidi tentoria Æthiopiæ]]: that is, by the ill deserts of their iniquities men become spiritually blackened and made like the devils, nay, the very tents of the devils, as the elect are the house and temple of God[[1 Cor 3:16||]][[1 Cor 3:17||]]. [[3:7|the curtains of the land of Madian shall be troubled|Turbabuntur pelles terræ Madian]] [*pelles*, literally "skins"]. The Septuagint translated: The tents of the land of Madian shall be afraid. Hence, according to Jerome, we must take the tents of the Ethiopians and of the Madianites to be the same men, who for their sins [[Wis 5:2|shall be troubled with terrible fear|turbabuntur timore horribili]] when they see that they are to be condemned. Spiritually, the skins of Madian are understood as self-will, the passions of the soul and the concupiscences of the flesh, with which the vicious, the rebellious and the disobedient cover, arm and clothe themselves. Some expound these words literally, thus: that for the iniquity of the destruction of the temple of Jerusalem the tents of Ethiopia and Madian were troubled, that is, overcome in war by the Persians and Medes; since the Ethiopians and Madianites, as they say, were with the king of Babylon at the destruction of the temple, and afterwards were slain with the Babylonians: from what source this can be proved, I do not know.

paras.t: Numquid in fluminibus iratus es, Domine? aut in fluminibus furor tuus? aut in mari indignatio tua? Quasi dicat: Tu, Deus justissime, non es inanimatis rebus iratus secundum se, sed in illis quædam opera facis ad liberationem tuorum, et destructionem pravorum, sicut in mari Rubro atque Jordane desiccatis populum Israel redemisti, et in mari illo Ægyptios submersisti. Qui ascendes super equos tuos. Istud ad litteram referri potest ad equitatus Persarum atque Medorum, qui Deo auxiliante Chaldæos vicerunt. Propter quod dicitur Deus eorum ascendisse equos, quoniam inspiravit eis ut equos contra Chaldæos ascenderent. Et quadrigæ tuæ, id est Persarum ac Medorum currus, sunt salvatio: id est, per currus et prælia horum liberati sunt filii Israel de Babylonica captivitate per Cyrum regem Persarum, ut scribitur in primo libro Esdræ.
paras.en: [[3:8|Wast thou angry, O Lord, with the rivers? or was thy wrath upon the rivers? or thy indignation in the sea?|Numquid in fluminibus iratus es, Domine? aut in fluminibus furor tuus? aut in mari indignatio tua?]] As if he said: Thou, O most just God, art not angry with lifeless things in themselves, but in them thou doest certain works for the deliverance of thine own and the destruction of the wicked, as when thou didst dry up the Red Sea[[Ex 14:1||]] and the Jordan[[Jos 3:1||]] and so redeem the people of Israel, and didst drown the Egyptians in that sea. [[3:8|Who will ride upon thy horses|Qui ascendes super equos tuos]]. This can be referred literally to the horsemen of the Persians and Medes, who with God's help conquered the Chaldeans. For this reason God is said to have mounted their horses, because he moved them to mount their horses against the Chaldeans. [[3:8|and thy chariots|Et quadrigæ tuæ]], that is, the chariots of the Persians and Medes, [[3:8|are salvation|salvatio]]: that is, through their chariots and battles the children of Israel were set free from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus king of the Persians, as is written in the first book of Esdras[[1 Esd 1:1||]].

paras.t: Suscitans suscitabis arcum tuum: id est, Persis et Medis dabis virtutem pugnandi ac sagittandi victoriose contra Chaldæos. Unde Septuaginta transtulerunt: Intendens, extendes arcum tuum. Quemadmodum ergo in Ezechiele gladium Nabuchodonosor regis appellat Dominus gladium suum, quia divinæ justitiæ exstitit exsecutor, Quum cœperit, inquiens, gladius meus volare; ita nunc quadrigæ et currus Persarum, itemque Medorum, dicuntur quadrigæ currusque Dei. Itaque, Suscitabis arcus istorum, ut impleas juramenta tribubus, quæ locutus es: id est, facies populo et tribubus Judæorum quæ eis per Moysen et Prophetas promisisti, videlicet quod quando in captivitate implorarent veraciter clementiam tuam, eriperes eos et ad terram promissionis eos reduceres. Hoc autem per Jeremiam Dominus specialiter promisit Judæis, quantum ad reditum a captivitate in Babylone. Hinc per Moysen et Nehemiam eis locutus est Deus: Si reversi fueritis ad me in toto corde vestro, etsi abducti fueritis ad extrema cœli, inde congregabo vos, et inducam vos in terram quam dedi patribus vestris. In fine versiculi hujus additur, Semper, quia a tempore Abrahæ cœpit ista promissio, et reiterata est sæpe; vel, Semper, tempore opportuno.
paras.en: [[3:9|Thou wilt surely take up thy bow|Suscitans suscitabis arcum tuum]]: that is, thou wilt give the Persians and Medes the strength to fight and shoot victoriously against the Chaldeans. Hence the Septuagint translated: Bending, thou wilt bend thy bow. As, then, in Ezechiel the Lord calls the sword of king Nabuchodonosor his own sword, because he was the executor of the divine justice, saying: [[Ezech 32:10|when my sword shall begin|Quum cœperit]], he says, [[Ezech 32:10|to fly|gladius meus volare]]; so now the chariots and cars of the Persians, and likewise of the Medes, are called the chariots and cars of God. Thus, thou wilt take up their bows, that thou mayest fulfil [[3:9|the oaths which thou hast spoken to the tribes|juramenta tribubus, quæ locutus es]]: that is, thou wilt do for the people and tribes of the Jews what thou didst promise them through Moses and the Prophets, namely that when in captivity they truly implored thy mercy, thou wouldst rescue them and bring them back to the land of promise. And this the Lord promised to the Jews specially through Jeremias, as regards the return from the captivity in Babylon[[Jer 29:10||]]. Hence God spoke to them through Moses and Nehemias: If you return to me with your whole heart[[Deut 30:2||]], [[2 Esd 1:9|though you should be led away to the uttermost parts of the world, I will gather you from thence|etsi abducti fueritis ad extrema cœli, inde congregabo vos]], and I will bring you into the land which I gave to your fathers[[Deut 30:5||]] [the margin gives Deut. xxx, 1–5, and II Esdr. i, 9; Denis's words are closest to 2 Esd 1:9]. At the end of this verse *Always* is added, because this promise began from the time of Abraham and was often repeated; or, *Always*, that is, at the fitting time.

3.title: Prosecutio expositionis hujus capituli tertii ab eo loco quo dicitur: Fluvios scindes terræ.
3.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this third chapter from the place where it is said: Thou wilt divide the rivers of the earth.

paras.t: Consequenter ad litteram Propheta prosequitur Chaldæorum dejectionem. Fluvios scindes terræ. Per flumina et aquas, frequenter intelliguntur reges et eorum exercitus, sicut testatur Isaias : Adducet Dominus super Judam aquas fluminis multas et fortes, regem Assyriorum et omnem gloriam ejus. Est igitur sensus, secundum Hieronymum : Reges et populum contra Judæos pugnantes disperges, o Domine. Vel, ut alii asserunt, intelligi potest de divisione Euphratæ fluvii, quem Persæ ac Medi in plures lacus partiti sunt, sicque per alveum principalem evacuatum ab aquis, ingressi sunt Babylonem : quod quia Deo inspirante fecerunt, Deus fecisse describitur.
paras.en: Next, according to the letter, the Prophet goes on with the overthrow of the Chaldeans. [[3:9|Thou wilt divide the rivers of the earth|Fluvios scindes terræ]]. By rivers and waters kings and their armies are often understood, as Isaias bears witness: [[Is 8:7|the Lord will bring upon them the waters of the river strong and many, the king of the Assyrians, and all his glory|Adducet Dominus super Judam aquas fluminis multas et fortes, regem Assyriorum et omnem gloriam ejus]] [Denis reads "upon Juda" where the Vulgate has "upon them"]. The sense, then, according to Jerome, is: Thou wilt scatter, O Lord, the kings and the people that fight against the Jews. Or, as others assert, it can be understood of the dividing of the river Euphrates, which the Persians and Medes parted into several lakes; and so, the main channel having been emptied of its waters, they entered Babylon. And because they did this by God's inspiration, God is described as having done it.

paras.t: Viderunt te, id est, omnipotentiam atque rigorem divinæ justitiæ per experientiam agnoverunt, et doluerunt montes, puta elati principes Babylonis, et ceteri qui populum tuum vastaverunt, quando a Persis et Medis occidebantur. Unde in libro Judicum habetur : Sic pereant inimici tui, Domine ; itemque in Psalmo, Confundantur et pereant, et cognoscant quia nomen tibi Dominus. Gurges aquarum transiit, id est, impetus persecutionis persequentium populum tuum, te operante, defecit ; vel sensus est, quod inundatio aquarum Euphratæ modo præfato cessavit.
paras.en: [[3:10|The mountains saw thee|Viderunt te]], that is, they came to know by experience the almighty power and the rigour of the divine justice, [[3:10|and were grieved|et doluerunt montes]]: the mountains, namely the proud princes of Babylon and the others who had laid waste thy people, when they were being slain by the Persians and Medes. Hence we have in the book of Judges: [[Judg 5:31|So let all thy enemies perish, O Lord|Sic pereant inimici tui, Domine]]; and likewise in the Psalm: [[Ps 82:18|let them be confounded and perish|Confundantur et pereant]], [[Ps 82:19|And let them know that the Lord is thy name|et cognoscant quia nomen tibi Dominus]]. [[3:10|The great body of waters passed away|Gurges aquarum transiit]], that is, the onslaught of the persecution of those who persecuted thy people failed, thou working it; or the sense is that the flood of the waters of the Euphrates ceased in the manner described above.

paras.t: Dedit abyssus vocem suam : id est, aqua prænominata cum quodam fragore et sonitu locum suum reliquit. Vel, Dedit vocem suam materialiter et occasionaliter, quia ex ejus divisione sumpserunt alii materiam laudandi divinam justitiam, prout in Psalmo cantatur : Valles abundabunt frumento ; clamabunt, etenim hymnum dicent. Sic namque inanimata Deum benedicere et laudare feruntur. Porro, secundum Hieronymum sensus est : Abyssus dedit vocem suam, id est, inferi laudaverunt te : quod de sanctis in limbo detentis forte intelligit ; vel quod de Chaldæorum damnatione lætati sunt dæmones, et quoad hoc, divinam justitiam approbarunt. Altitudo manus suas levavit : id est, superni atque angelici spiritus, interioribus manibus de divinæ justitiæ exsecutione plaudendo, Deum glorificarunt. Hinc in Apocalypsi spiritualis Babylonis destructione descripta, inducitur : Exsultate, cœli et sancti Apostoli et Prophetæ, quoniam judicavit Deus judicium vestrum. Vel sensus est, quod Deus altissimus, qui est summa et prima sublimitas, manus suas levavit, id est, potestatem suam exercuit contra Chaldæos.
paras.en: [[3:10|The deep put forth its voice|Dedit abyssus vocem suam]]: that is, the water named above left its place with a certain crash and roar. Or, it [[3:10|put forth its voice|Dedit vocem suam]] materially and occasionally [that is, not by uttering a sound itself, but by giving others matter and occasion for praise], because from its dividing others took matter for praising the divine justice, as is sung in the Psalm: [[Ps 64:14|the vales shall abound with corn: they shall shout, yea they shall sing a hymn|Valles abundabunt frumento ; clamabunt, etenim hymnum dicent]]. For in this way things without life are said to bless and praise God. Further, according to Jerome the sense is: The deep put forth its voice, that is, those below praised thee; which he perhaps understands of the saints held in limbo; or that the demons rejoiced at the damnation of the Chaldeans and, so far as this goes, approved the divine justice. [[3:10|The deep lifted up its hands|Altitudo manus suas levavit]] [the Latin *altitudo* is "the height", which Denis reads here; the Douay-Rheims has "the deep"]: that is, the spirits on high, the angelic spirits, clapping with their inward hands over the carrying out of the divine justice, glorified God. Hence in the Apocalypse, when the destruction of the spiritual Babylon has been described, it is added: [[Apoc 18:20|Rejoice|Exsultate]], [[Apoc 18:20|thou heaven and ye holy apostles and prophets|cœli et sancti Apostoli et Prophetæ]], [[Apoc 18:20|For God hath judged your judgment|quoniam judicavit Deus judicium vestrum]]. Or the sense is that God most high, who is the supreme and first height, lifted up his hands, that is, exercised his power against the Chaldeans.

paras.t: Sol et luna steterunt in habitaculo suo. Consuetudo Scripturæ est, ut luminaria cœli, quæ in ministerium hominum condita sunt, obscurari et mœrere dicantur, dum hominibus adversa magna contingunt, ut patet in Ezechiele, Joele, aliisque Prophetis ; quum vero hominibus prospera accidunt, fulgere et quasi reflorere feruntur. Quemadmodum ergo in devastatione Judæorum dirissima a Chaldæis, sol et luna obscurata dicuntur per quamdam metaphoram, juxta illud Joelis, Sol et luna obtenebrati sunt, et stellæ retraxerunt splendorem suum ; sic in liberatione eorum a captivitate Chaldaica, sol et luna ad pristinum sunt reversa vigorem, non quod in se ipsis mutata sunt quantum ad modum præfatum. Sic igitur loco præsenti denuntiata Judæorum liberatione, sol et luna in habitaculo suo stetisse scribuntur, id est, in gradu atque vigore vel splendore consueto fuerunt : hoc est, sic de eorum fulgore gavisi sunt Judæi, ut olim tempore prosperitatis ac pacis : ita quod Stare, non dicit hic cessationem a motu, sed exsistentiam stabilem, sicut communiter dicimus, Ille stetit Romæ tot annis. Unde Septuaginta transtulerunt : Elevatus est sol, quoad pristini vigoris receptionem, modo nunc explanato ; et luna stetit in ordine suo, id est in pristino gradu ac modo.
paras.en: [[3:11|The sun and the moon stood still in their habitation|Sol et luna steterunt in habitaculo suo]]. It is the custom of Scripture that the lights of heaven, which were made for the service of men, are said to be darkened and to mourn when great adversities befall men, as is plain in Ezechiel[[Ezech 32:7||]][[Ezech 32:8||]], Joel[[Joel 2:10||]][[Joel 2:31||]][[Joel 3:15||]] and other Prophets[[Is 13:10||]]; but when prosperity comes to men, they are said to shine and as it were to bloom again. As therefore, in the most cruel laying waste of the Jews by the Chaldeans, the sun and moon are said by a kind of metaphor to be darkened, according to that of Joel: [[Joel 3:15|The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their shining|Sol et luna obtenebrati sunt, et stellæ retraxerunt splendorem suum]] [the same words stand in Joel 2:10]; so in their deliverance from the Chaldean captivity the sun and moon returned to their former vigour: not that they were changed in themselves in the manner spoken of. So then here, where the deliverance of the Jews is foretold, the sun and moon are written to have stood in their habitation, that is, they were in their accustomed degree and vigour or brightness: that is, the Jews rejoiced in their shining as once in the time of prosperity and peace. So that *to stand* here does not mean ceasing from motion, but a steady abiding [the Douay-Rheims "stood still" takes the word in the sense Denis here sets aside], as we commonly say: He stood [that is, stayed] at Rome so many years. Hence the Septuagint translated: The sun was lifted up (as to the recovery of its former vigour, in the way just explained), and the moon stood in her order, that is, in her former degree and manner.

paras.t: In luce sagittarum tuarum ibunt : id est, sol et luna solito cursu movebuntur, quoad ipsos Judæos, eorum utilitati suis motibus deserviendo ut olim, in luce sagittarum tuarum, id est mediantibus splendentibus Persarum ac Medorum sagittis, quas contra Chaldæos miserunt, atque per hoc populum Israel de illorum manibus redemerunt. Simili sensu subjungitur : in splendore fulgurantis hastæ tuæ, id est mediantibus fulgidis hastis Persarum : quorum sagittæ et hastæ dicuntur esse Dei, prout præcedenti articulo equi et currus eorum, Dei esse dicuntur. Vel sensus est, quod Chaldæi ibunt, id est, peribunt et esse cessabunt, virtute sagittarum atque hastarum jam præfatarum.
paras.en: [[3:11|in the light of thy arrows, they shall go|In luce sagittarum tuarum ibunt]]: that is, the sun and moon will move in their wonted course in respect of the Jews themselves, serving their profit by their motions as of old, [[3:11|in the light of thy arrows|in luce sagittarum tuarum]], that is, by means of the shining arrows of the Persians and Medes, which they shot against the Chaldeans, and by this redeemed the people of Israel out of their hands. In a like sense it is added: [[3:11|in the brightness of thy glittering spear|in splendore fulgurantis hastæ tuæ]], that is, by means of the gleaming spears of the Persians; whose arrows and spears are said to be God's, as in the preceding article their horses and chariots are said to be God's[[3:8||]]. Or the sense is that the Chaldeans shall go, that is, shall perish and cease to be [*ibunt*, "they shall go", taken as *peribunt*, "they shall perish"], by the power of the arrows and spears just mentioned.

paras.t: In fremitu, id est in districtione tuæ justitiæ, vel in ira et animositate Persarum, conculcabis terram, id est populum Chaldæorum seu Babyloniæ regionem ; et in furore, id est in rigore tuæ justitiæ, obstupefacies gentes Chaldæis auxiliantes.
paras.en: [[3:12|In thy anger|In fremitu]] [*fremitus*, literally a roaring or growling], that is, in the strictness of thy justice, or in the wrath and fierceness of the Persians, [[3:12|thou wilt tread the earth under foot|conculcabis terram]], that is, the people of the Chaldeans, or the country of Babylonia; and [[3:12|in thy wrath|in furore]], that is, in the rigour of thy justice, [[3:12|thou wilt astonish the nations|obstupefacies gentes]] that help the Chaldeans.
