paras.t: Egressus es, non locum mutando, qui incircumscriptibilis invariabilisque consistis, sed tuam potentiam ostendendo, et aliquid de novo manifeste operando, in salutem populi tui, id est ad salvandum Judæos de captivitate sæpe præfata, in salutem cum christo tuo, id est cum Cyro rege Persarum, ut quidam exponunt : qui dicitur christus Dei, id est in regem a Deo electus, juxta illud in Isaia, Hæc dicit Dominus christo meo Cyro. Hieronymus autem exponit de Domino nostro Jesu Christo, cum quo in hunc mundum per incarnationem veniente, venit et Pater per gratiæ suæ operationem multiplicem, sicut et Filius is loquitur : Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit ; et Pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Et rursus : Pater (inquit) in me manens, ipse facit opera ; et, Pater non reliquit me solum. Venit ergo Pater in salutem generis humani cum Christo suo Domino salvatore : nam et opera summæ Trinitatis sunt indivisa ; et Filius, Omnia (ait) quæ facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit.
paras.en: [[3:13|Thou wentest forth|Egressus es]], not by changing place, for thou art uncircumscribable and unchangeable, but by showing thy power and by working something new openly, [[3:13|for the salvation of thy people|in salutem populi tui]], that is, to save the Jews from the captivity so often mentioned, [[3:13|for salvation with thy Christ|in salutem cum christo tuo]], that is, with Cyrus king of the Persians, as some explain it; who is called the christ of God, that is, chosen by God to be king, according to that in Isaias: [[Is 45:1|Thus saith the Lord to my anointed Cyrus|Hæc dicit Dominus christo meo Cyro]] [the Latin has *christo*, the same word as "Christ" in this verse]. But Jerome explains it of our Lord Jesus Christ: with whom, as he came into this world by the Incarnation, the Father also came by the manifold working of his grace; as the Son himself also says: [[John 14:23|If any one love me, he will keep my word. And my Father will love him and we will come to him and will make our abode with him|Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit ; et Pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus]]. And again: [[John 14:10|the Father|Pater]], he says, [[John 14:10|who abideth in me, he doth the works|in me manens, ipse facit opera]]; and: [[John 8:29|he hath not left me alone|Pater non reliquit me solum]] [Denis puts "the Father" for "he"]. The Father therefore came for the salvation of mankind with his Christ, the Lord and Saviour: for the works of the supreme Trinity are undivided; and the Son says: [[John 5:19|what things soever he doth|Omnia]], he says, [[John 5:19|these the Son also doth in like manner|quæ facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit]].

paras.t: Percussisti caput de domo impii, id est, Balthasar regem Babylonis per Persas occidisti, et de palatio suo ejecisti. Vel caput istud intelligitur diabolus a Christo dejectus, seu Antichristus ab ipso dejiciendus. Denudasti fundamentum ejus usque ad collum, id est, abscondita et secreta capitis hujus totaliter confudisti, et revelasti, et destruxisti. Machinationes enim diaboli Christus aperuit, ita ut dicat Apostolus : Non ignoramus cogitationes diaboli ; et denuo, Alii datur discretio spirituum. Omnia quoque abscondita regis Balthasar Chaldæi scrutati sunt.
paras.en: [[3:13|Thou struckest the head of the house of the wicked|Percussisti caput de domo impii]], that is, thou didst slay Baltasar king of Babylon by means of the Persians[[Dan 5:30||]], and didst cast him out of his palace. Or this head is understood as the devil, cast down by Christ, or Antichrist, who is to be cast down by him. [[3:13|thou hast laid bare his foundation even to the neck|Denudasti fundamentum ejus usque ad collum]], that is, thou hast utterly confounded, revealed and destroyed the hidden and secret things of this head. For Christ laid open the devices of the devil, so that the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 2:11|we are not ignorant of his devices|Non ignoramus cogitationes diaboli]] [Denis has "the devil's devices"]; and again: [[1 Cor 12:10|to another, the discerning of spirits|Alii datur discretio spirituum]]. They also searched out all the hidden things of the Chaldean king Baltasar.

paras.t: Maledixisti sceptris ejus, id est, regnis ac dominationibus regis Babylonis maledixisti, et capiti bellatorum ejus, id est principi militiæ, venientibus ut turbo ad dispergendum me, id est, qui copiose et impetuose venerunt ad destruendum populum Judæorum. Non est autem necesse, hæc omnia referri præcise ad eosdem numero, quoniam sacra Scriptura sæpe loquitur de diversis quasi de eisdem, quia ad unum populum pertinent. Rex autem Babylonis et ejus princeps militiæ, qui Jerusalem destruxerunt, fuerunt Nabuchodonosor et Nabuzardan, qui non fuerunt a Persis et Medis occisi. Exsultatio eorum sicut ejus qui devorat pauperem in abscondito : id est, præfati principes sic gloriati sunt populum Israel opprimendo, quemadmodum gloriatur crudelis egenum occulte dilanians et affligens : quoniam sine timore hoc fecerunt crudeliter, nec Deum omnia inspicientem tanquam judicem attenderunt.
paras.en: [[3:14|Thou hast cursed his sceptres|Maledixisti sceptris ejus]], that is, thou hast cursed the kingdoms and dominions of the king of Babylon, and [[3:14|the head of his warriors|capiti bellatorum ejus]], that is, the chief of the soldiery, [[3:14|them that came out as a whirlwind to scatter me|venientibus ut turbo ad dispergendum me]], that is, who came in great numbers and with violence to destroy the people of the Jews. Now it is not necessary that all these things be referred precisely to the same persons in number, since Holy Scripture often speaks of different persons as though of the same, because they belong to one people. For the king of Babylon and the chief of his soldiery who destroyed Jerusalem were Nabuchodonosor and Nabuzardan[[4 Kings 25:1||]], who were not slain by the Persians and Medes. [[3:14|Their joy was like that of him that devoureth the poor man in secret|Exsultatio eorum sicut ejus qui devorat pauperem in abscondito]]: that is, the princes spoken of so gloried in oppressing the people of Israel as a cruel man glories in secretly tearing and afflicting the needy; for they did this cruelly and without fear, and paid no heed to God, who beholds all things, as their judge.

paras.t: Viam fecisti in mari equis tuis, id est, equis atque equitibus Persarum et Medorum dedisti iter per arentem Euphratæ alveum, aqua ejus hinc inde educta. Ideo subditur : in luto aquarum multarum. Aqua enim educta, terra alvei fuit aliquo modo lutosa. Euphraten autem nominat mare, more loquendi Hebraico, quo quælibet grandis aquarum collectio dicitur mare, secundum illud Genesis : Congregationes aquarum appellavit Deus maria.
paras.en: [[3:15|Thou madest a way in the sea for thy horses|Viam fecisti in mari equis tuis]], that is, to the horses and horsemen of the Persians and Medes thou gavest a road through the dry bed of the Euphrates, its water having been drawn off on either side. Therefore it is added: [[3:15|in the mud of many waters|in luto aquarum multarum]]. For when the water had been drawn off, the ground of the bed was somewhat muddy. Now he calls the Euphrates a sea, after the Hebrew manner of speech, in which any great gathering of waters is called a sea, according to that of Genesis: [[Gen 1:10|the gathering together of the waters, he called Seas|Congregationes aquarum appellavit Deus maria]].

paras.t: Audivi a te, Domine, per spiritum prophetiæ comminationes tuas adversus Chaldæos, et conturbatus est venter meus, id est, dolor seu timor animæ tantus fuit, quod redundavit in corpus. Vel per ventrem intelligitur mens, quæ est uterus spiritualis, de quo Salomon ait : Fili, accipe doctrinam, quæ tibi pulchra erit, quum in ventre tuo tenueris eam. De quo Pater testatur in Psalmo ad Filium : Ex utero ante luciferum genui te. A voce, id est ab auditu verborum tuorum, contremuerunt labia mea : in tantum formidavi rigorem justitiæ tuæ. Quamvis autem Habacuc de Chaldæorum dejectione gavisus sit, secundum unam considerationem, prout fuit occasio liberationis Judæorum, tamen secundum aliquas considerationes, expavit ac doluit, et ex amore naturæ, eorum gravissimæ calamitati compassus est, sicut superius ex Isaia ostensum est. Nam et Isaias, descripta Babylonis destructione, inter cetera dicit : Elanguit cor meum, tenebræ stupefecerunt me.
paras.en: [[3:16|I have heard|Audivi]] from thee, O Lord, through the spirit of prophecy, thy threats against the Chaldeans, [[3:16|and my bowels were troubled|et conturbatus est venter meus]], that is, the grief or fear of my soul was so great that it overflowed into the body. Or by the bowels [Latin *venter*, "belly" or "womb"] the mind is understood, which is the spiritual womb, of which Solomon says: My son, receive instruction[[Prov 22:17||]], [[Prov 22:18|Which shall be beautiful for thee, if thou keep it in thy bowels|quæ tibi pulchra erit, quum in ventre tuo tenueris eam]]; and of which the Father bears witness in the Psalm to the Son: [[Ps 109:3|from the womb before the day star I begot thee|Ex utero ante luciferum genui te]]. [[3:16|at the voice|A voce]], that is, at the hearing of thy words, [[3:16|my lips trembled|contremuerunt labia mea]]: so greatly did I dread the rigour of thy justice. Now although Habacuc rejoiced at the overthrow of the Chaldeans in one respect, inasmuch as it was the occasion of the deliverance of the Jews, yet in some other respects he was dismayed and grieved, and from natural love he suffered with them in their most grievous calamity, as was shown above from Isaias [the margin refers to Art. II]. For Isaias too, having described the destruction of Babylon, says among other things: [[Is 21:4|My heart failed, darkness amazed me|Elanguit cor meum, tenebræ stupefecerunt me]].

paras.t: Ingrediatur putredo in ossibus meis, et subter me scateat: id est, tribulatio et infirmitas, quantumcumque gravis me apprehendat, dummodo tibi placuerit, et gratiæ tuæ subventione supposita, qua patientiam largiaris. Ut requiescam in die tribulationis, id est, tempore destructionis Babyloniorum cesset captivitatis meæ pressura, et in spe liberationis repausem. Ut ascendam ad populum accinctum nostrum, id est, Babylone destructa, de licentia Cyri regis Persarum, pergam a Chaldæa in Judæam simul cum populo Judæorum in Judæam revertente, armato atque ad prælium præparato : videlicet cum viris præclaris Esdra, Nehemia, Zorobabel, et Jesu filio Josedec, qui propter insidias hostium erant ad pugnandum dispositi, ut patet in Esdra. Hæc dicit Habacuc non in sua, sed in Judæorum persona. Ipse enim in captivitate prædicta non fuit, sed in Judæa remansit, ut legitur in Daniele.
paras.en: [[3:16|Let rottenness enter into my bones, and swarm under me|Ingrediatur putredo in ossibus meis, et subter me scateat]]: that is, let tribulation and sickness, however grievous, lay hold on me, provided it please thee, and the help of thy grace be put beneath it, by which thou mayest grant patience. [[3:16|That I may rest in the day of tribulation|Ut requiescam in die tribulationis]], that is, that in the time of the destruction of the Babylonians the oppression of my captivity may cease, and I may rest in the hope of deliverance. [[3:16|that I may go up to our people that are girded|Ut ascendam ad populum accinctum nostrum]], that is, that, Babylon being destroyed, I may go with leave of Cyrus king of the Persians from Chaldea into Judea, together with the people of the Jews returning into Judea, armed and prepared for battle: namely with those illustrious men Esdras, Nehemias, Zorobabel, and Josue the son of Josedec, who because of the snares of their enemies were set in readiness to fight, as is plain in Esdras[[2 Esd 4:1||]] [the margin gives II Esdr. iv, that is, the book of Nehemias, where the builders stand armed, vv. 16–18]. Habacuc says these things not in his own person but in the person of the Jews. For he himself was not in the said captivity, but remained in Judea, as we read in Daniel[[Dan 14:32||]].

paras.t: Consequenter Propheta causam assignat, cur in die tribulationis Babyloniorum tam vehementer requiescere et consolari rogaverit. Ficus enim non florebit, et non erit germen in vineis, id est, arbores fici et vites steriles erunt. Mentietur opus olivæ, id est, speratus olivarum fructus præstolantes decipiet, et per modum mentientis se habebit, non oriendo, ut aliquando prætendebat; et arva non afferent cibum : pro quo Septuaginta transtulerunt, Campi non facient escas. Per quæ omnia insinuatur sterilitas territorii Chaldæorum, cujus campos et arbores Persæ et Medi vastabant. Et aliqui asserunt, quod sterilitas ista fuit plaga a Deo inflicta ante Persarum adventum. Certum est autem, quod talis sterilitas expugnationem vastitatemque terræ soleat concomitari. Abscindetur de ovili pecus : id est, a stabulis Chaldæorum auferentur jumenta eorum, vel per hostes, vel alimentorum penuriis. Ideo subditur : et non erit armentum, id est pecorum multitudo, in præsepibus, in quibus cibos accipere solent. Sicque Chaldæis adhuc manentibus, vel in terra illorum exsistentibus, deerit carnium usus.
paras.en: Next the Prophet gives the reason why, in the day of the Babylonians' tribulation, he asked so earnestly to rest and be comforted. [[3:17|For the fig tree shall not blossom|Ficus enim non florebit]], [[3:17|and there shall be no spring in the vines|et non erit germen in vineis]], that is, the fig trees and the vines will be barren. [[3:17|The labour of the olive tree shall fail|Mentietur opus olivæ]] [*mentietur*, literally "shall lie"], that is, the hoped-for fruit of the olives will deceive those who wait for it, and will behave like one who lies, by not coming forth as it once promised; [[3:17|and the fields shall yield no food|et arva non afferent cibum]]: for which the Septuagint translated: The plains shall not make food. By all these things is signified the barrenness of the territory of the Chaldeans, whose fields and trees the Persians and Medes laid waste. And some assert that this barrenness was a plague inflicted by God before the coming of the Persians. But it is certain that such barrenness is wont to go with the storming and wasting of a land. [[3:17|the flock shall be cut off from the fold|Abscindetur de ovili pecus]]: that is, their beasts will be taken away from the stalls of the Chaldeans, either by the enemy or through want of fodder. Therefore it is added: [[3:17|and there shall be no herd|et non erit armentum]], that is, no multitude of cattle, [[3:17|in the stalls|in præsepibus]], in which they are wont to take their food. And so, while the Chaldeans still remain, or dwell in their own land, they will lack the use of meat.

paras.t: Postremo, quoniam ex consideratione punitionis pravorum, solent electi cautiores melioresque fieri, atque ad gratiarum actionem et laudem divinam provocari (quemadmodum in Proverbiis Salomon adstruit, Pestilente flagellato, homo sapientior erit : etenim, felix quem faciunt aliena damna peritum), Propheta Deum laudans, ejusque æquitati applaudens, subjungit : Ego autem, illis sic pereuntibus, in Domino gaudebo, in contemplatione et dilectione ejus et beneficiorum ac promissorum ipsius, in actibus quoque virtuosis ei placentibus : sicut et virgo Maria, Exsultavit, inquit, spiritus meus in Deo salutari meo; et Anna in libro primo Regum, Exsultavit cor meum in Domino. Et exsultabo, id est, signa interioris lætitiæ exterius demonstrabo, in Deo Jesu, id est salvatore meo. Unde Septuaginta transtulerunt : Gaudebo super Deo salvatore meo. Potestque nomen Jesu hoc loco sumi proprie atque communiter : intentio namque Prophetæ finalis ac principalis, est loqui vel de ipso Salvatore Filio Dei, et ejus quam nobis impendit salute, vel de Cyro rege Persarum, et Judæorum per eum liberatione, in quantum fuerunt figura Christi regis et suæ salvationis.
paras.en: Lastly, since from considering the punishment of the wicked the elect are wont to become more wary and better, and to be stirred to thanksgiving and to the praise of God (as Solomon declares in Proverbs: [[Prov 19:25|The wicked man being scourged|Pestilente flagellato]], a man [[Prov 19:25|shall be wiser|sapientior erit]] [the Vulgate has "the fool" where Denis has "a man"]; and indeed, happy is he whom others' losses make wary [a proverb, not from Scripture]), the Prophet, praising God and applauding his equity, adds: [[3:18|But I|Ego autem]], while they thus perish, [[3:18|will rejoice in the Lord|in Domino gaudebo]], in contemplating and loving him and his benefits and promises, and also in virtuous acts pleasing to him: as also the Virgin Mary: [[Luke 1:47|my spirit hath rejoiced|Exsultavit]], she says, [[Luke 1:47|in God my Saviour|spiritus meus in Deo salutari meo]]; and Anna in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 2:1|My heart hath rejoiced in the Lord|Exsultavit cor meum in Domino]]. [[3:18|and I will joy|Et exsultabo]], that is, I will show outwardly the signs of inward gladness, [[3:18|in God my Jesus|in Deo Jesu]], that is, my Saviour. Hence the Septuagint translated: I will rejoice in God my Saviour. And the name *Jesus* can be taken here both properly and in the common sense [that is, both as the proper name of Christ and in its general meaning, "saviour"]: for the final and principal intention of the Prophet is to speak either of the Saviour himself, the Son of God, and of the salvation which he bestows on us, or of Cyrus king of the Persians and the deliverance of the Jews through him, inasmuch as these were a figure of Christ the king and of his salvation.

paras.t: Deus Dominus fortitudo mea, non formalis, sed effectiva, id est confirmator meus, et totius roboris mei causa præcipua : cujus virtute liberatus est populus Israel de Babylone; de quo ait Psalmista, Diligam te, Domine, fortitudo mea; qui et testatur, Sine me nihil potestis facere. Et ponet pedes meos quasi cervorum, id est, agilitatem bene agendi mihi præstabit, et populum Israel in terram Judææ expedite reducet. Loquitur autem Propheta in persona populi sui.
paras.en: [[3:19|The Lord God is my strength|Deus Dominus fortitudo mea]]: not formal but effective [that is, not the strength that is in me as a quality, but the cause that makes me strong], that is, my strengthener and the chief cause of all my might; by whose power the people of Israel was delivered from Babylon; of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 17:2|I will love thee, O Lord, my strength|Diligam te, Domine, fortitudo mea]]; and who himself declares: [[John 15:5|without me you can do nothing|Sine me nihil potestis facere]]. [[3:19|and he will make my feet like the feet of harts|Et ponet pedes meos quasi cervorum]], that is, he will give me nimbleness in doing well, and will swiftly bring the people of Israel back into the land of Judea. For the Prophet speaks in the person of his people.

paras.t: Et super excelsa mea, id est ad loca Judææ sublimia et montuosa, deducet me victor Deus omnipotens. De quo in Numeris Balaam contestatur : Dominus Deus Israel cum eo est, et clangor victoriæ regis in illo est. De quo loquitur Jephthe : Quæ Dominus Deus noster victor obtinuit, in nostram cedent partem. Ipse est rex ille omnipotens, cujus voluntati nedum non prævalere, sed nec resistere quispiam potest. Vel, Super excelsa mea, id est ad virtutum præclarissima opera, sive ad pristinam dignitatem, honorem et gloriam, puta ad sacerdotium, sacrificia, templi reparationem, principatum ac potestatem, deducet me victor. Hæc enim post reditum de Babylone recuperaverunt Judæi, ut patet in Esdra et libris Machabæorum ac aliis locis. Vel, ad regna cœlestia deducet me victor Christus, de quo legitur in Apocalypsi, Vicit leo de tribu Juda : sicque verba ista accipi possunt in persona eorum quos Christus de limbo perduxit ad patriam.
paras.en: And [[3:19|upon my high places|super excelsa mea]], that is, to the lofty and mountainous places of Judea, [[3:19|he the conqueror will lead me|deducet me victor]], God almighty. Of whom Balaam bears witness in Numbers: [[Num 23:21|The Lord his God is with him, and the sound of the victory of the king in him|Dominus Deus Israel cum eo est, et clangor victoriæ regis in illo est]] [Denis has "the Lord God of Israel"]. Of whom Jephte speaks: [[Judg 11:24|what the Lord our God hath obtained by conquest, shall be our possession|Quæ Dominus Deus noster victor obtinuit, in nostram cedent partem]] [the Latin has *victor obtinuit*, "obtained as conqueror", the word of this verse]. He is that almighty king whose will no one can prevail against, nor even resist[[Esth 13:9||]]. Or, [[3:19|upon my high places|Super excelsa mea]], that is, to the most excellent works of the virtues, or to their former dignity, honour and glory, namely to the priesthood, the sacrifices, the restoring of the temple, princely rule and power, [[3:19|he the conqueror will lead me|deducet me victor]]. For these things the Jews recovered after the return from Babylon, as is plain in Esdras and the books of the Machabees and in other places. Or, to the heavenly kingdom Christ the conqueror will lead me, of whom we read in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 5:5|the lion of the tribe of Juda|leo de tribu Juda]] [[Apoc 5:5|hath prevailed|Vicit]] [Latin *vicit*, "hath conquered", answering to *victor*]; and so these words can be taken in the person of those whom Christ led out of limbo to the fatherland.

paras.t: Sic ergo deducet me in psalmis canentem, id est ei gratias referentem, eumque laudantem : sicut in Ecclesiastico scribitur : Laudabit usque ad mortem anima mea Dominum, quoniam eruis sustinentes te, Domine, et liberas eos de omni angustia.
paras.en: So then he [[3:19|will lead me|deducet me]] [[3:19|singing psalms|in psalmis canentem]], that is, giving thanks to him and praising him; as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 51:8|My soul shall praise the Lord even to death|Laudabit usque ad mortem anima mea Dominum]], [[Ecclus 51:12|How thou deliverest them that wait for thee, O Lord, and savest them|quoniam eruis sustinentes te, Domine, et liberas eos]] from every distress [the margin reads Eccli. ii, 8, 12, for li (51); Denis ends "from every distress" where the Vulgate has "out of the hands of the nations"].

3.title: De expositione exordii cantici hujus secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum, et expositio ejusdem cantici tropologica seu moralis.
3.title_en: On the exposition of the opening of this canticle according to the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, and the tropological or moral exposition of the same canticle.

paras.t: QUONIAM Tractus missalis Officii in die Parasceves, ex hoc cantico sumptus est secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum, quæ etiam translatio a translatione Hieronymi in hoc passu satis distat, congruit principium cantici hujus secundum illorum translationem pertranseundo exponere.
paras.en: Since the Tract of the Mass on the day of Parasceve [the day of preparation, that is, Good Friday] is taken from this canticle according to the translation of the Seventy Interpreters [the Septuagint], a translation which in this passage differs a good deal from Jerome's, it is fitting to expound the beginning of this canticle briefly, in passing, according to their translation.

paras.t: Titulus autem, quem Septuaginta capitulo huic præmittunt, est hic : Oratio Habacuc prophetæ cum cantico : quia in isto capitulo agitur de Christi adventu et salvatione, pro qua Deum cum hymnis, psalmis et canticis spiritualibus orare debemus.
paras.en: Now the title which the Seventy set before this chapter is this: [[3:1|A PRAYER OF Habakkuk THE PROPHET|Oratio Habacuc prophetæ]] with a canticle [so the Septuagint; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have 'for ignorances']: because this chapter treats of the coming of Christ and of salvation, for which we ought to pray to God with hymns, psalms and spiritual canticles[[Eph 5:19||]].

paras.t: Itaque Septuaginta transtulerunt : Domine, audivi auditum tuum, et timui : quod supra satis expositum est. Domine, consideravi opera tua, id est mirabilia tua judicia, effectus tuæ justitiæ, ordinem creaturarum, gubernationem universi, miracula quæ a principio mundi fecisti, dona gratiarum, hominum dispositionem, et qualiter genus humanum liberare decreveris, et obstupui (vel expavi), id est, ad mentis excessum perductus sum, et præ admiratione defeci, clamans cum divino Apostolo : O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus! Porro, secundum Hieronymum, quod Septuaginta dixerunt, Consideravi, et obstupui, in Hebraico non habetur. Verum, secundum Augustinum, qui in libro de Civitate Dei in pluribus locis valde commendat translationem Septuaginta interpretum, asserens eos prophetali spiritu transtulisse, et ex divino instinctu addidisse quæ addiderunt, tenendum est quod ista et reliqua quæ addiderunt, Deo inspirante locuti sunt.
paras.en: So the Seventy translated: [[3:2|O Lord, I have heard thy hearing, and was afraid|Domine, audivi auditum tuum, et timui]]; which has been explained sufficiently above. *O Lord, I have considered thy works* [the Septuagint; the Douay-Rheims has only 'O Lord, thy work'], that is, thy wonderful judgments, the effects of thy justice, the order of creatures, the government of the universe, the miracles which thou hast wrought from the beginning of the world, the gifts of graces, the ordering of men, and how thou hast decreed to set mankind free; *and I was astonished* (or *I was afraid*), that is, I was carried out of myself in ecstasy of mind, and fainted for wonder, crying out with the divine Apostle: [[Rom 11:33|O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!|O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus!]] Further, according to Jerome, what the Seventy said, *I have considered, and I was astonished*, is not in the Hebrew. But according to Augustine, who in many places in his book *The City of God* strongly commends the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, declaring that they translated by a prophetic spirit and added what they added by divine prompting, we must hold that these words, and the rest that they added, they spoke by the inspiration of God.

paras.t: In medio duorum animalium cognosceris (vel innotesces), id est inter duos populos ex quibus collecta est sancta Ecclesia, utpote in medio conversorum ex Judaismo et paganismo. De quibus loquitur Zacharias, Consilium pacis erit inter duos illos ; et Apostolus, Ipse est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum. Quemadmodum enim duo parietes in lapide angulari concurrunt et copulantur; ita in Christo summo lapide angulari, duo populi isti facti sunt unum mysticum corpus, unumque templum, de quo dicit Zacharias : Ipse ædificabit templum Domino. Vel duo animalia intelliguntur duo Testamenta, vere vivifica, gratiæ vitam spirantia. Quidam per duo animalia intelligunt duos latrones inter quos suspensus est Christus atque innotuit, centurione dicente, Vere Filius Dei erat iste ; quando et omnis turba eorum qui aderant, et videbant quæ tempore passionis fiebant, percutientes pectora sua revertebantur. Postremo, non desunt qui per duo animalia intelligunt bovem et asinum quos Joseph secum duxit in Bethlehem, Christi nativitate instante : inter quos infantulus Jesus in præsepio positus, agnitus fuit a Matre et Joseph, vel ab istis jumentis, secundum similitudinem quamdam. Ad quod referunt illud Isaiæ : Cognovit bos possessorem suum, et asinus præsepe domini sui. Expositio autem eorum qui per duo animalia intelligunt Filium et Spiritum Sanctum, eo quod Pater per Filium et Spiritum Sanctum cognoscatur (qui etiam in Isaia per duo Seraphim Filium et Spiritum Sanctum accipiunt), est suspecta, nec placet, præsertim quum canticum istud specialiter de persona Filii tractet.
paras.en: *In the midst of two living creatures thou shalt be known* (or *thou shalt be made known*) [this is the Septuagint's reading; the Douay-Rheims, following the Hebrew, has 'in the midst of the years'], that is, between the two peoples from which holy Church is gathered, namely in the midst of those converted from Judaism and from paganism. Of these Zacharias speaks: [[Zach 6:13|the counsel of peace shall be between them both|Consilium pacis erit inter duos illos]]; and the Apostle: [[Eph 2:14|he is our peace, who hath made both one|Ipse est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum]]. For as two walls meet and are joined in the corner stone, so in Christ, the chief corner stone[[Eph 2:20||]], these two peoples have been made one mystical body and one temple, of which Zacharias says: [[Zach 6:13|he shall build a temple to the Lord|Ipse ædificabit templum Domino]] [Denis's verb, *ædificabit*, is that of the verse before, Zach 6:12]. Or by the two living creatures are understood the two Testaments, truly life-giving, breathing the life of grace. Some understand by the two living creatures the two thieves between whom Christ was hung[[Matt 27:38||]] and became known, when the centurion said, [[Matt 27:54|Indeed this was the Son of God|Vere Filius Dei erat iste]]; when also [[Luke 23:48|all the multitude of them|omnis turba eorum]] that were present, and saw the things that were done in the time of the passion, [[Luke 23:48|returned, striking their breasts|percutientes pectora sua revertebantur]] [the margin gives no reference for these words, which are from Luke 23:48]. Lastly, there are those who understand by the two living creatures the ox and the ass which Joseph took with him to Bethlehem when Christ's birth was at hand: between which the infant Jesus, laid in the manger[[Luke 2:12||]], was recognized by his Mother and Joseph, or, after a certain likeness, by these beasts. To this they refer that saying of Isaias: [[Is 1:3|The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib|Cognovit bos possessorem suum, et asinus præsepe domini sui]]. But the exposition of those who understand by the two living creatures the Son and the Holy Ghost, because the Father is known through the Son and the Holy Ghost (and they also take the two Seraphim in Isaias[[Is 6:2||]] as the Son and the Holy Ghost), is suspect and does not please, especially since this canticle treats specially of the person of the Son.

paras.t: Quum appropinquaverint anni, cognosceris : id est, tempore gratiæ seu evangelicæ legis clarius te agnoscent fideles : quia ut ait Apostolus, Ubi venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum. Et in prima sua Canonica ait Joannes : Scimus quoniam Filius Dei venit, et dedit nobis sensum, ut cognoscamus Deum verum. Ante enim notus erat in Judæa Deus, sed adveniente tempore gratiæ, ad unius veri Dei cultum atque notitiam totus conversus est mundus. Quum advenerit tempus præordinatum a Deo, ostenderis, id est, fidelibus innotesces. Hoc est tempus incarnationis et conversationis Christi in mundo, itemque evangelicæ prædicationis : de quo loquitur Paulus, Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis; et Baruch, Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est. Unde et Christus ait ad Patrem : Ego te clarificavi super terram, manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus, quos dedisti mihi. — Quod vero nunc dictum est, Quum advenerit tempus, ostenderis, secundum Hieronymum, in Hebræo non ponitur, sed a Septuaginta interpretibus est additum.
paras.en: *When the years draw near, thou shalt be known* [the Septuagint again; the Douay-Rheims has 'In the midst of the years thou shalt make it known']: that is, in the time of grace or of the Gospel law the faithful will know thee more clearly; because, as the Apostle says, [[Gal 4:4|when the fulness of the time was come, God sent his Son|Ubi venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum]]. And John says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 5:20|we know that the Son of God is come. And he hath given us understanding that we may know the true God|Scimus quoniam Filius Dei venit, et dedit nobis sensum, ut cognoscamus Deum verum]]. For before, God was known in Judea, but when the time of grace came, the whole world was converted to the worship and knowledge of the one true God. *When the time is come* that God foreordained, *thou shalt be shown*, that is, thou shalt be made known to the faithful. This is the time of the incarnation of Christ and of his dwelling among men in the world, and likewise of the preaching of the Gospel: of which Paul speaks, [[2 Cor 6:2|Behold, now is the acceptable time: behold, now is the day of salvation|Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis]]; and Baruch, [[Bar 3:38|Afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men|Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est]]. Hence Christ too says to the Father: [[John 17:4|I have glorified thee on the earth|Ego te clarificavi super terram]], [[John 17:6|I have manifested thy name to the men whom thou hast given me|manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus, quos dedisti mihi]]. But what has just been said, *When the time is come, thou shalt be shown*, is, according to Jerome, not in the Hebrew, but was added by the Seventy Interpreters.

paras.t: Deus a Theman veniet, id est ab austro, secundum Hieronymum : quod jam satis expositum reor. Et Sanctus de monte umbroso et condenso : id est, Christus Sanctus Sanctorum in mundum hunc venit de paradiso cœlesti ac summo, pleno vivis uberrimisque arboribus, puta angelicis atque supernis virtutibus. Vel mons iste umbrosus, est Deus Pater incomprehensibilis et perfectus, qui majestate sua omnia tegit et operit, de cujus sinu Filius descendit in mundum, non locum transmutans, sed naturam humanam assumens. Quidam dicunt : Deus a Libano veniet : et redit in idem. Per Libanum nempe, qui candidatio interpretatur, splendidissimus iste paradisus, vel superpulcherrimus Deus Pater, seu lux divina inaccessibilis, congrue designatur.
paras.en: *God will come from Theman* [so the Septuagint; the Douay-Rheims has 'from the south'], that is, from the south, according to Jerome; which I think has been explained sufficiently already; [[3:3|and the holy one|Et Sanctus]] *from the shady and thickly wooded mountain* [the Septuagint; the Douay-Rheims has 'from mount Pharan']: that is, Christ, the Holy of Holies, came into this world from the heavenly and most high paradise, full of living and most fruitful trees, namely the angelic and heavenly powers. Or this shady mountain is God the Father, incomprehensible and perfect, who covers and overshadows all things with his majesty, from whose bosom the Son came down into the world, not by changing place but by taking human nature. Some say: *God will come from Libanus*; and it comes to the same thing. For by Libanus, which is interpreted *whitening* [*candidatio*, a making white or bright], this most splendid paradise, or God the Father, beautiful beyond all beauty, or the divine light inaccessible, is fittingly signified.

paras.t: Quum ergo ex his pateat, in cantico isto tam manifeste tractari prophetatumque esse de Christo ac ejus mysteriis, præsertim secundum Septuaginta interpretum translationem, certum est quosdam in hujus cantici explanatione nimis superficiales et litterales consistere, qui omnia ista, et pene omnia quæ sequuntur, ad litteram referunt ad Babyloniæ destructionem.
paras.en: Since, then, it is plain from these things that this canticle treats and prophesies so manifestly of Christ and his mysteries, especially according to the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, it is certain that some, in explaining this canticle, remain too superficial and literal: those who refer all these things, and nearly all that follow, literally to the destruction of Babylon.

paras.t: Expositio tropologica. NUNC ad moralitatem eundum est. Unde quilibet contemplativus fidelis, divinorum operum considerator industrius, dicere potest : Domine, audivi, auribus mentis et corporis, auditionem tuam, id est sacræ Scripturæ sermones, et verba divinitus revelata : de quibus loquitur Isaias : Domine, quis credidit auditui nostro? et timui, filiali et casto timore, qui est fuga mali culpæ, ne Deus offendatur : sicut timuit Psalmista, qui ait : A verbis tuis formidavit cor meum. Itaque cum reverentia et timore audienda sunt verba Dei. Unde Josiæ quarto Regum libro promittitur : Quia timuisti a facie verborum quæ audisti, et perterritum est cor tuum, in pace collegeris. Et Jeremias : Factus sum, inquit, velut vir ebrius a facie verborum sanctorum Dei. Quis enim non timeat, audiens illud, De omni verbo otioso reddent homines rationem; et illud, Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis; et, Nescit homo an sit dignus amore vel odio, sed omnia in futurum reservantur incerta; illud etiam, Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum? Ideo sanctus Job profitetur : Considerans Deum, timore sollicitor. Alibi quoque dicit Scriptura : Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus.
paras.en: Tropological exposition. Now we must go on to the moral sense. Any faithful contemplative, then, a diligent considerer of the divine works, can say: [[3:2|O Lord, I have heard|Domine, audivi]], with the ears of mind and body, [[3:2|thy hearing|auditionem tuam]], that is, the discourses of sacred Scripture and the words divinely revealed, of which Isaias speaks: Lord, who [[Is 53:1|hath believed our report|quis credidit auditui nostro]]? [the word 'Lord' is not in Isaias, but is added where the verse is cited at John 12:38 and Rom 10:16]; [[3:2|and was afraid|et timui]], with filial and chaste fear, which is the flight from the evil of fault [that is, of sin, as distinct from the evil of punishment], lest God be offended; as the Psalmist feared, who says: [[Ps 118:161|my heart hath been in awe of thy words|A verbis tuis formidavit cor meum]]. So the words of God are to be heard with reverence and fear. Hence it is promised to Josias in the fourth book of Kings: Because thou hast feared at the presence of the words which thou hast heard, and [[4 Kings 22:19|thy heart hath been moved to fear|perterritum est cor tuum]], thou shalt be gathered in peace[[4 Kings 22:20||]] [Denis gives the sense of 4 Kings 22:18–20 rather than its words]. And Jeremias: [[Jer 23:9|I am become|Factus sum]], he says, [[Jer 23:9|as a drunken man|velut vir ebrius]] [[Jer 23:9|at the presence of his holy words|a facie verborum sanctorum Dei]]. For who would not fear, hearing that saying: Of [[Matt 12:36|every idle word that men shall speak, they shall render an account|omni verbo otioso reddent homines rationem]]; and that other: [[Heb 10:31|It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God|Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis]]; and: [[Eccles 9:1|man knoweth not whether he be worthy of love, or hatred|Nescit homo an sit dignus amore vel odio]], [[Eccles 9:2|But all things are kept uncertain for the time to come|sed omnia in futurum reservantur incerta]]; and that also: [[Matt 25:41|Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire|Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum]]? Therefore holy Job declares: [[Job 23:15|when I consider him, I am made pensive with fear|Considerans Deum, timore sollicitor]]. Elsewhere too Scripture says: [[Prov 28:14|Blessed is the man that is always fearful|Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus]].

paras.t: Domine, opus tuum est nostra redemptio, et omne bonum quod agimus. Non enim sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid ex nobis; sed Deus est qui operatur in nobis velle et perficere. In medio annorum, videlicet anno gratiæ ac evangelicæ legis, qui inter annum legis Mosaicæ annumque gloriæ medius est, vivifica illud, animas nostras actualiter redimendo, nosque in juventute nostra in bonis operibus inflammando, et omne quod agimus per caritatem infusam spiritualiter vivificando.
paras.en: [[3:2|O Lord, thy work|Domine, opus tuum]] is our redemption, and every good thing that we do. For [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves|Non enim sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid ex nobis]]; but [[Phil 2:13|it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish|Deus est qui operatur in nobis velle et perficere]]. [[3:2|in the midst of the years|In medio annorum]], namely in the year of grace and of the Gospel law, which stands midway between the year of the Mosaic law and the year of glory, [[3:2|bring it to life|vivifica illud]], by actually redeeming our souls, kindling us in our youth to good works, and spiritually quickening all that we do through infused charity.

paras.t: In medio annorum, jam dicto, notum facies nostræ redemptionis vel justificationis opus, dando gratiam magnam ac evidentem, ita ut electi tui inter ceteros quasi sidera verbo et exemplo resplendeant. Quum iratus fueris, tuos electos nunc castigando, atque pro suis peccatis multipliciter corripiendo, hostibusque tradendo, misericordiæ recordaberis, peccata dimittendo, gratiam refundendo, consolationem præstando, citra condignum ulciscendo, et cum tribulatione proventum faciendo. Ideo cantamus in Psalmo : Numquid in æternum irasceris nobis? Deus, tu conversus vivificabis nos. Et item : Si iniquitates observaveris, Domine, Domine, quis sustinebit? Hinc in Threnis Jeremias testatur : Misericordiæ Domini, quia non sumus consumpti; quia non defecerunt miserationes ejus. Denique in libro Tobiæ scriptum est: Benedictum est nomen tuum, Deus patrum nostrorum, quia quum iratus fueris, misericordiam facies, et in tempore tribulationis peccata dimittis his qui invocant te. Et rursum : Non delectaris, Domine, in perditionibus nostris, quia post tempestatem tranquillum facis, et post fletum exsultationem infundis.
paras.en: [[3:2|In the midst of the years|In medio annorum]], the year just spoken of, [[3:2|thou shalt make it known|notum facies]], the work of our redemption or justification, by giving great and evident grace, so that thy elect shine out among the rest like stars by word and example; [[3:2|when thou art angry|Quum iratus fueris]], now chastising thy elect, correcting them in many ways for their sins and handing them over to enemies, [[3:2|thou wilt remember mercy|misericordiæ recordaberis]], forgiving sins, pouring back grace, granting consolation, punishing short of what is deserved, and with the tribulation making a way out[[1 Cor 10:13||]]. Therefore we sing in the Psalm: [[Ps 84:6|Wilt thou be angry with us for ever|Numquid in æternum irasceris nobis]]? [[Ps 84:7|Thou wilt turn, O God, and bring us to life|Deus, tu conversus vivificabis nos]]. And again: [[Ps 129:3|If thou, O Lord, wilt mark iniquities: Lord, who shall stand it|Si iniquitates observaveris, Domine, Domine, quis sustinebit?]]? Hence Jeremias testifies in the Lamentations: [[Lam 3:22|The mercies of the Lord that we are not consumed: because his commiserations have not failed|Misericordiæ Domini, quia non sumus consumpti; quia non defecerunt miserationes ejus]]. Lastly, it is written in the book of Tobias: [[Tob 3:13|Blessed is thy name, O God of our fathers, who when thou hast been angry, wilt shew mercy, and in the time of tribulation forgivest the sins of them that call upon thee|Benedictum est nomen tuum, Deus patrum nostrorum, quia quum iratus fueris, misericordiam facies, et in tempore tribulationis peccata dimittis his qui invocant te]]. And again: [[Tob 3:22|thou art not delighted in our being lost, because after a storm thou makest a calm, and after tears and weeping thou pourest in joyfulness|Non delectaris, Domine, in perditionibus nostris, quia post tempestatem tranquillum facis, et post fletum exsultationem infundis]].

paras.t: Deus ab austro veniet, et Sanctus de monte Pharan. Deum semper precemur, ut juxta sensum præhabitum ad nos venire, jugiterque nobiscum manere dignetur. Per austrum quoque intelliguntur homines lumine gratiæ radiosi, et a Deo sublimiter docti. De illis igitur venit Deus ad alios, dum gratiam sibi concessam aliis communicare, eosque ad Deum reducere eniuntur. Operuit cœlos, id est contemplativos, quorum conversatio est in cœlis, gloria ejus, dicente in eorum persona Apostolo : Nos autem revelata facie, gloriam Dei speculantes. Et laudis ejus plena est terra, id est activi qui circa terrena versantur. Terra quoque, id est terreni, carnales et reprobi, frequenter in ore pleni sunt laudibus Dei, sed mente et opere non cessant inhonorare Deum atque offendere. De quibus Dominus protestatur : Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me.
paras.en: [[3:3|God will come from the south, and the holy one from mount Pharan|Deus ab austro veniet, et Sanctus de monte Pharan]]. Let us always pray God that, in the sense given before, he may deign to come to us and to abide with us continually. By the south, too, are understood men radiant with the light of grace and sublimely taught by God. From these, then, God comes to others, when they strive to share with others the grace granted to them and to lead them back to God. [[3:3|His glory|gloria ejus]] [[3:3|covered the heavens|Operuit cœlos]], that is, the contemplatives, whose [[Phil 3:20|conversation is in heaven|conversatio est in cœlis]], the Apostle saying in their person: [[2 Cor 3:18|But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with open face|Nos autem revelata facie, gloriam Dei speculantes]]. [[3:3|and the earth is full of his praise|Et laudis ejus plena est terra]], that is, the active, who are busied about earthly things. The earth, too, that is, the earthly, carnal and reprobate, are often full of God's praises in their mouths, but in mind and deed do not cease to dishonour and offend God. Of these the Lord declares: [[Matt 15:8|This people honoureth me with their lips: but their heart is far from me|Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me]][[Is 29:13||]].

paras.t: Splendor ejus, id est fulgor gratiæ Dei, ut lux erit, id est clarus et candidus sicut lumen solare, cui in multis assimilatur, tenebras mentis fugando, animam fecundando, torporem acediæ auferendo, intima cordis ornando. Insuper splendor gratiæ assimilatur lumini gloriæ, cujus est inchoatio quædam. Cornua in manibus ejus. Cornua ista possunt accipi in bono, pro elevatis et sanctis virtutibus animæ : quæ sunt in manibus Dei, quia in ejus potestate est eas dare, conservare, auferre, et consummare. Itemque in malo, pro nostris superbiis, ac ceteris quibus contra Deum et proximum intumescimus vitiis, juxta illud in Job : Quid te elevat cor tuum, et quasi magna cogitans, attonitos habes oculos? quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus? Istis comminatur sermo divinus in Amos : Væ qui dicitis : Numquid non in fortitudine nostra assumpsimus nobis cornua? Hæc quoque cornua nostra sunt in manibus Dei, qui superbos ad nutum dejicere potest, quemadmodum scriptum est : Deus confringet capita inimicorum suorum, verticem capilli perambulantium in delictis suis. Ibi abscondita est fortitudo ejus : quia in bonis cornibus electorum, virtus divina frequenter agit occulte; sed et superborum dejectionem sæpe diutius differendo, videtur Deus quasi non attendere, aut non omnipotens esse.
paras.en: [[3:4|His brightness|Splendor ejus]], that is, the radiance of God's grace, [[3:4|shall be as the light|ut lux erit]], that is, clear and white like the light of the sun, to which it is likened in many ways: in putting to flight the darkness of the mind, making the soul fruitful, taking away the torpor of sloth [*acedia*, the weariness of spiritual things], and adorning the inmost heart. Moreover, the brightness of grace is likened to the light of glory, of which it is a kind of beginning. [[3:4|horns are in his hands|Cornua in manibus ejus]]. These horns can be taken in a good sense, for the lofty and holy virtues of the soul, which are in the hands of God, because it is in his power to give, preserve, take away and perfect them. And likewise in a bad sense, for our prides and the other vices by which we swell against God and our neighbour, according to that in Job: [[Job 15:12|Why doth thy heart elevate thee, and why dost thou stare with thy eyes, as if they were thinking great things?|Quid te elevat cor tuum, et quasi magna cogitans, attonitos habes oculos?]] [[Job 15:13|Why doth thy spirit swell against God|quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus]]? Against these the divine word threatens in Amos: [[Amos 6:1|Woe|Væ]] to [[Amos 6:14|you that say: Have we not taken unto us horns by our own strength?|qui dicitis : Numquid non in fortitudine nostra assumpsimus nobis cornua?]] These horns of ours too are in the hands of God, who can cast down the proud at his nod, as it is written: [[Ps 67:22|God shall break the heads of his enemies: the hairy crown of them that walk on in their sins|Deus confringet capita inimicorum suorum, verticem capilli perambulantium in delictis suis]] [the margin gives no reference; the words are Ps 67:22]. [[3:4|There is his strength hid|Ibi abscondita est fortitudo ejus]]: because in the good horns of the elect the divine power often works hiddenly; and also, by often putting off for a long while the casting down of the proud, God seems as it were not to heed, or not to be almighty.

paras.t: Ante faciem ejus ibit mors : quia quum Deus per gratiæ suæ adspirationem intraverit mentem, mors fugiet peccati. Tunc et egredietur diabolus. Christus enim fortem armatum, puta diabolum, alligavit, et vasa ejus quotidie diripit, faciens eos templum Spiritus Sancti, qui erant vasa diaboli.
paras.en: [[3:5|Death shall go before his face|Ante faciem ejus ibit mors]]: because when God, by the breathing of his grace, has entered the mind, the death of sin will flee. Then too [[3:5|the devil shall go forth|egredietur diabolus]]. For Christ has bound the strong man armed[[Luke 11:21||]], that is, the devil, and daily plunders his vessels[[Luke 11:22||]], making those who were vessels of the devil a temple of the Holy Ghost[[1 Cor 3:16||]].

paras.t: Stetit et mensus est terram. Christus in mundo hoc cum discipulis vivens, mensus est terram in qua prædicarent Apostoli, mittendo eos ad solos Judæos. Porro post passionem et Spiritus Sancti missionem, mensus est terram gentilium, ad diversas nationes mittendo Apostolos. Adspexit misericorditer, et contriti sunt montes sæculi ab itineribus æternitatis ejus : quia exemplis et documentis Salvatoris, quibus humilitatem præcipue commendavit, humiliati sunt multi magnatum, Christum humiliter imitati.
paras.en: [[3:6|He stood and measured the earth|Stetit et mensus est terram]]. Christ, living in this world with his disciples, measured the land in which the Apostles were to preach, sending them to the Jews alone[[Matt 10:5||]][[Matt 10:6||]]. But after the passion and the sending of the Holy Ghost, he measured the land of the Gentiles, sending the Apostles to the various nations. [[3:6|He beheld|Adspexit]] in mercy, [[3:6|and the ancient mountains were crushed to pieces|et contriti sunt montes sæculi]] [[3:6|by the journeys of his eternity|ab itineribus æternitatis ejus]] [Denis joins the 'mountains of the world' to the 'journeys of his eternity', passing over the words between]: because by the examples and teachings of the Saviour, in which he especially commended humility, many of the great have been humbled, humbly imitating Christ.

paras.t: Numquid in fluminibus iratus es, Domine? aut in fluminibus furor tuus? In Scripturis crebro per flumina designantur perversi ac turbulenti, eorumque vitia instar fluminum redundantia. Sic enim habetur in Psalmo : Elevaverunt flumina fluctus suos. Et Jeremias regem atque exercitum Chaldæorum nomine fluvii exprimit. Istis fluminibus irascitur Dominus. Interdum autem per flumina designantur electi ac docti, aqua sapientiæ pleni, et gratia copiosi, qui fluenta doctrinæ transfundunt in alios, et rivis salutaris scientiæ rigant corda eorum. Tales etiam dicuntur fontes in Psalmo. Istis non irascitur Deus. Flumina quoque vocantur divina charismata, juxta illud : Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ ; et alibi, Fluminis impetus lætificat civitatem Dei. Aut in mari indignatio tua? id est, sæcularis vitæ hominibus, amaritudine et fluctibus vitiorum repletis, juste indignaris. De quibus in Isaia legitur : Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest.
paras.en: [[3:8|Wast thou angry, O Lord, with the rivers? or was thy wrath upon the rivers?|Numquid in fluminibus iratus es, Domine? aut in fluminibus furor tuus?]] In the Scriptures the rivers often signify the perverse and turbulent, and their vices, which overflow like rivers. For so it is in the Psalm: [[Ps 92:3|The floods have lifted up their waves|Elevaverunt flumina fluctus suos]]. And Jeremias denotes the king and army of the Chaldeans by the name of a river[[Jer 2:18||]]. With these rivers the Lord is angry. But sometimes the rivers signify the elect and learned, full of the water of wisdom[[Ecclus 15:3||]] and abounding in grace, who pour the streams of doctrine into others and water their hearts with the brooks of saving knowledge. Such are also called fountains in the Psalm[[Ps 67:27||]]. With these God is not angry. The divine gifts [*charismata*, the free gifts of grace] are also called rivers, according to that saying: [[John 7:38|He that believeth in me|Qui credit in me]], [[John 7:38|Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water|flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ]]; and elsewhere: [[Ps 45:5|The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful|Fluminis impetus lætificat civitatem Dei]] [the margin gives no reference for these two; they are John 7:38 and Ps 45:5]. [[3:8|or thy indignation in the sea?|Aut in mari indignatio tua?]] that is, thou art justly indignant with the men of worldly life, filled with the bitterness and the waves of vices. Of whom we read in Isaias: [[Is 57:20|the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest|Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]].

paras.t: Qui ascendes super equos tuos, id est animas sanctas, secundum Hieronymum, vel prædicatores nomen Domini undique circumferentes ac prædicantes : super quos Deus ascendit per virtutis et gratiæ suæ effectum. Et quadrigæ tuæ sunt salvatio, id est Evangelistæ, vel etiam angeli sancti, Deum in se recipientes, portantes, atque ad homines deferentes. De quibus cantatur in Psalmo : Currus Dei decem millibus multiplex millia lætantium, Dominus in eis. De his equis et curribus Dominus loquitur in Isaia : Adducent omnes fratres vestros in equis et quadrigis, et in lecticis et mulis, et in carrucis ad montem sanctum meum Jerusalem. Per hos ergo currus operatur Dominus aliorum salutem, sicut ait Apostolus : Dei cooperatores sumus.
paras.en: [[3:8|Who will ride upon thy horses|Qui ascendes super equos tuos]], that is, holy souls, according to Jerome, or preachers who carry the name of the Lord about everywhere and preach it: upon whom God mounts by the working of his power and grace. [[3:8|and thy chariots are salvation|Et quadrigæ tuæ sunt salvatio]], that is, the Evangelists, or also the holy angels, who receive God into themselves, bear him, and bring him to men. Of these we sing in the Psalm: [[Ps 67:18|The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands; thousands of them that rejoice: the Lord is among them|Currus Dei decem millibus multiplex millia lætantium, Dominus in eis]]. Of these horses and chariots the Lord speaks in Isaias: [[Is 66:20|they shall bring all your brethren|Adducent omnes fratres vestros]] [[Is 66:20|upon horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and on mules, and in coaches, to my holy mountain Jerusalem|in equis et quadrigis, et in lecticis et mulis, et in carrucis ad montem sanctum meum Jerusalem]]. Through these chariots, then, the Lord works the salvation of others, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 3:9|we are God's coadjutors|Dei cooperatores sumus]].

paras.t: Suscitans suscitabis arcum tuum, id est verbum tuum seu sacram Scripturam, cujus ignita eloquia, te agente, audientium penetrant corda, et caritatis vulnere sauciant, ita ut dicant : Caritate vulneratus sum ; et, Amore langueo. Unde et Christus de se ipso loquitur per Isaiam : Posuit me Dominus quasi sagittam electam. Hunc arcum suscitat Deus, dum prædicatoribus et servis suis electis infundit gratiam loquendi aliis fructuose ac fervide, secundum quod orat Apostolus : Ut detur mihi sermo in apertione oris mei. Et in Isaia legitur : Dominus dedit mihi linguam eruditam, ut sciam sustentare eum qui lassus est, verbo. Hoc autem, o Domine, faciendo, suscitabis juramenta tribubus, quæ locutus es, id est, bona gratiæ, quæ gentibus promisisti, eorum conversionem per Prophetas prænuntiando, donabis; deinde hereditatem cœlestem conferes eis, ut promisisti.
paras.en: [[3:9|Thou wilt surely take up thy bow|Suscitans suscitabis arcum tuum]] [*suscitabis*, literally 'thou wilt rouse up'], that is, thy word or sacred Scripture, whose fiery words, by thy working, pierce the hearts of the hearers and wound them with the wound of charity, so that they say: I am wounded with charity[[Cant 4:9||]] [the margin gives Cant 4:9, where the Vulgate has 'Thou hast wounded my heart'; Denis's words are not the Vulgate's]; and: [[Cant 2:5|I languish with love|Amore langueo]]. Hence Christ too speaks of himself through Isaias: The Lord [[Is 49:2|hath made me as a chosen arrow|Posuit me Dominus quasi sagittam electam]]. This bow God rouses up when he pours into his preachers and chosen servants the grace of speaking to others fruitfully and fervently, as the Apostle prays: [[Eph 6:19|that speech may be given me, that I may open my mouth|Ut detur mihi sermo in apertione oris mei]]. And in Isaias we read: [[Is 50:4|The Lord hath given me a learned tongue, that I should know how to uphold by word him that is weary|Dominus dedit mihi linguam eruditam, ut sciam sustentare eum qui lassus est, verbo]]. And in doing this, O Lord, thou wilt rouse up [[3:9|the oaths which thou hast spoken to the tribes|juramenta tribubus, quæ locutus es]], that is, thou wilt bestow the goods of grace which thou didst promise to the nations, foretelling their conversion through the Prophets; and afterwards thou wilt confer on them the heavenly inheritance, as thou hast promised.

paras.t: Fluvios scindes terræ : id est, de ipsa Ecclesia quosdam separabis, et mittes ad aliorum informationem per omnes terminos terræ. Sic enim misit Apostolos, aliosque discipulos, prædicatores, doctores. Hinc in Actibus legitur Spiritus Sanctus dixisse : Segregate mihi Paulum et Barnabam in opus ad quod assumpsi eos. Et per Isaiam Dominus ait : Ponam in deserto (id est in gentilitate) flumina; et iterum, Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas. Isti sunt fluvii boni, de quibus cantamus : In Ecclesiis benedicite Deo Domino de fontibus Israel.
paras.en: [[3:9|Thou wilt divide the rivers of the earth|Fluvios scindes terræ]]: that is, thou wilt set some apart from the Church itself, and send them to instruct others through all the ends of the earth. For so he sent the Apostles and other disciples, preachers and doctors. Hence we read in the Acts that the Holy Ghost said: [[Acts 13:2|Separate me Saul and Barnabas, for the work whereunto I have taken them|Segregate mihi Paulum et Barnabam in opus ad quod assumpsi eos]] [Denis has 'Paul', where the Vulgate has 'Saul']. And through Isaias the Lord says: [[Is 43:19|I will make|Ponam]] [[Is 43:19|in the wilderness|in deserto]] (that is, among the Gentiles) [[Is 43:19|rivers|flumina]]; and again: [[Is 55:1|All you that thirst, come to the waters|Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas]]. These are the good rivers of which we sing: [[Ps 67:27|In the churches bless ye God the Lord, from the fountains of Israel|In Ecclesiis benedicite Deo Domino de fontibus Israel]].

paras.t: Viderunt te, et doluerunt montes. Hoc dupliciter accipi potest : primo, de superbis atque potentibus sæculi ad fidem conversis, quia per fidem Deum viderunt, atque de suis excessibus pœnitentiam dignam fecerunt; secundo, de infidelibus ac tyrannis, qui mirabilia Dei videntes, doluerunt de promulgatione fidei christianæ. Gurges aquarum transiit : id est, istorum persecutio contra fideles cessavit, vel si est, cito finietur, videlicet simul cum vita præsenti, quæ brevis est, vel ante. Vel sensus est, quod documentorum rivuli ad alios devenerunt. Dedit abyssus vocem suam : id est, corda quorumdam, instar pelagi inscrutabilia, fide Christi recepta, Deum super ejus misericordia laudaverunt. Altitudo manus suas levavit : quia et sæculares principes ad fidem conversi, manibus in cælum elevatis, Deum precati sunt, sicut in Threnis Jeremias hortatur : Levemus corda nostra cum manibus in cælos ad Dominum. Itemque Apostolus : Volo, inquit, viros orare in omni loco, levantes puras manus. Porro sæculares principes perfidi, manus suas contra Ecclesiam extenderunt.
paras.en: [[3:10|The mountains saw thee, and were grieved|Viderunt te, et doluerunt montes]]. This can be taken in two ways: first, of the proud and mighty of the world converted to the faith, because through faith they saw God and did worthy penance for their excesses; secondly, of unbelievers and tyrants, who, seeing the wonders of God, grieved at the spreading of the Christian faith. [[3:10|the great body of waters passed away|Gurges aquarum transiit]]: that is, their persecution of the faithful has ceased, or, if it still goes on, it will soon be ended, namely together with the present life, which is short, or before. Or the sense is that the streams of teaching have come down to others. [[3:10|The deep put forth its voice|Dedit abyssus vocem suam]]: that is, the hearts of some, unsearchable like the open sea, having received the faith of Christ, have praised God for his mercy. [[3:10|the deep lifted up its hands|Altitudo manus suas levavit]] [*altitudo*, 'the height', which Denis takes of the great ones of the world]: because the princes of the world too, converted to the faith, have prayed to God with hands lifted up to heaven, as Jeremias exhorts in the Lamentations: [[Lam 3:41|Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens|Levemus corda nostra cum manibus in cælos ad Dominum]]. And likewise the Apostle: [[1 Tim 2:8|I will|Volo]], he says, [[1 Tim 2:8|that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands|viros orare in omni loco, levantes puras manus]]. But the faithless princes of the world have stretched out their hands against the Church.

paras.t: Sol, id est Christus sol sapientiæ atque justitiæ, de quo impii asserunt, Sol intelligentiæ non est exortus nobis, et luna, id est Virgo Christifera, vel ipsa Ecclesia, steterunt in habitaculo suo, id est in ecclesiastica unitate, vel in ipso omnium rerum ultimo fine, in quo omnis Sanctorum quiescit intentio atque affectio, quasi in tabernaculo firmo, secundum quod Salomon dicit : Turris fortissima nomen Domini ; ad ipsum currit justus, et exaltabitur. Unde orat vir sanctus : Esto mihi in Deum protectorem, et in locum munitum. Vel habitaculum istud est regnum cælorum, in quo stat Ecclesia militans per spem et cordis amorem. Ubi namque thesaurus, ibi et cor ; et non minus (ut dicitur) est anima ubi amat, quam ubi animat. Vel, sol et luna sunt religiosi et sæculares fideles, in Ecclesia militanti, fide et opere concorditer permanentes. — Secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum ita habetur : Elevatus est sol, scilicet Christus in sua ascensione ; et luna stetit in ordine suo, id est, Ecclesia, præcipue primitiva, ordinate vixit, et stabilis fuit, secundum Christi doctrinam, consilia et præcepta, malens occidi quam ab ordine æquitatis recedere.
paras.en: [[3:11|The sun|Sol]], that is, Christ, the sun of wisdom and of justice, of whom the wicked say, [[Wis 5:6|the sun of understanding hath not risen upon us|Sol intelligentiæ non est exortus nobis]] [the margin gives no reference; the words are Wis 5:6], [[3:11|and the moon|et luna]], that is, the Virgin who bore Christ, or the Church herself, [[3:11|stood still in their habitation|steterunt in habitaculo suo]], that is, in the unity of the Church, or in the very last end of all things, in which every intention and affection of the Saints rests as in a firm tabernacle; according to what Solomon says: [[Prov 18:10|The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the just runneth to it, and shall be exalted|Turris fortissima nomen Domini ; ad ipsum currit justus, et exaltabitur]]. Hence a holy man prays: [[Ps 70:3|Be thou unto me a God, a protector, and a place of strength|Esto mihi in Deum protectorem, et in locum munitum]]. Or this habitation is the kingdom of heaven, in which the Church militant stands by hope and by the love of the heart. For where the treasure is, there is the heart also; and (as the saying goes) the soul is no less where it loves than where it gives life [*ubi amat … ubi animat*: a play on *amat*, 'loves', and *animat*, 'animates']. Or the sun and moon are the religious and the secular faithful in the Church militant, abiding together in concord in faith and works. According to the translation of the Seventy Interpreters it reads thus: *The sun was lifted up*, namely Christ in his ascension; *and the moon stood in her order*, that is, the Church, especially the primitive Church, lived in good order and was steadfast according to the teaching, counsels and precepts of Christ, choosing rather to be slain than to depart from the order of justice [the Douay-Rheims, with the Vulgate, has 'The sun and the moon stood still in their habitation'].

paras.t: In luce sagittarum tuarum, id est in veritate eloquiorum divinorum vel prædicatorum fidelium : de quibus jam dictum est. De quibus et apud Isaiam Dominus ait : Mittam ex eis qui salvati fuerint, ad gentes in mare, in Africam et Lydiam, tenentes sagittam, in Italiam et Græciam, ad insulas longe ; et annuntiabunt gloriam meam gentibus. Ibunt fideles de virtute in virtutem, de bono in melius, de via ad patriam, in splendore fulgurantis hastæ tuæ, id est spiritualium armorum vel divinarum comminationum. Unde Septuaginta transtulerunt : In splendore coruscationis armorum tuorum. Propter quod ad Ephesios hortatur Apostolus : Induite vos armaturam Dei, ut possitis stare adversus insidias diaboli.
paras.en: [[3:11|in the light of thy arrows|In luce sagittarum tuarum]], that is, in the truth of the divine words, or of faithful preachers, of whom we have already spoken. Of whom the Lord also says in Isaias: [[Is 66:19|I will send of them that shall be saved, to the Gentiles into the sea, into Africa, and Lydia them that draw the bow: into Italy, and Greece, to the islands afar off|Mittam ex eis qui salvati fuerint, ad gentes in mare, in Africam et Lydiam, tenentes sagittam, in Italiam et Græciam, ad insulas longe]]; [[Is 66:19|And they shall declare my glory to the Gentiles|et annuntiabunt gloriam meam gentibus]]. [[3:11|they shall go|Ibunt]], that is, the faithful, [[Ps 83:8|from virtue to virtue|de virtute in virtutem]], from good to better, from the way to the fatherland, [[3:11|in the brightness of thy glittering spear|in splendore fulgurantis hastæ tuæ]], that is, of spiritual arms or of divine threats. Hence the Seventy translated: *In the brightness of the flashing of thy arms*. For which reason the Apostle exhorts the Ephesians: [[Eph 6:11|Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil|Induite vos armaturam Dei, ut possitis stare adversus insidias diaboli]].

paras.t: In fremitu, id est districtissimo tuo judicio, conculcabis terram, damnando terrenos, præsertim in die novissimo. Egressus es in salutem populi tui. Dominus enim fortitudo plebis suæ, et ipse dux noster est et propugnator, juxta illud : In exercitu nostro Deus dux est; et in Psalmo, Deduxisti me, quia factus es spes mea ; in salutem cum christo tuo, id est quolibet Christiano electo spiritualiter uncto.
paras.en: [[3:12|In thy anger|In fremitu]] [*in fremitu*, literally 'in roaring'], that is, by thy most strict judgment, [[3:12|thou wilt tread the earth under foot|conculcabis terram]], by condemning the earthly-minded, especially on the last day. [[3:13|Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people|Egressus es in salutem populi tui]]. [[Ps 27:8|The Lord is the strength of his people|Dominus enim fortitudo plebis suæ]], and he himself is our leader and champion, according to that saying: [[2 Par 13:12|God is the leader in our army|In exercitu nostro Deus dux est]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 60:3|Thou hast conducted me|Deduxisti me]], [[Ps 60:4|For thou hast been my hope|quia factus es spes mea]]; [[3:13|for salvation with thy Christ|in salutem cum christo tuo]], that is, with every elect Christian, spiritually anointed [*christus* means 'anointed'].

paras.t: Percussisti caput, id est principem pravum, de domo impii, id est de grege impiorum subditorum ipsius, privando eum principatu, potestate seu vita, juxta illud Ecclesiastici : Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis. Et apud Lucam : Dispersit superbos mente cordis sui ; deposuit potentes de sede, et exaltavit humiles. Ipse quippe transfert regna atque constituit, sicut in Daniele asseritur. Denudasti fundamentum ejus usque ad collum, id est, funditus destrues illos : secundum quod in libro Sapientiæ scribitur, Dirumpet inflatos, et eos a fundamentis suis commovebit, et usque ad supremum desolabuntur.
paras.en: [[3:13|Thou struckest the head|Percussisti caput]], that is, the wicked prince, [[3:13|of the house of the wicked|de domo impii]], that is, from the flock of his wicked subjects, depriving him of his princedom, his power or his life; according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:17|God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes, and hath set up the meek in their stead|Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis]]. And in Luke: [[Luke 1:51|he hath scattered the proud in the conceit of their heart|Dispersit superbos mente cordis sui]]; [[Luke 1:52|He hath put down the mighty from their seat and hath exalted the humble|deposuit potentes de sede, et exaltavit humiles]]. For he [[Dan 2:21|taketh away kingdoms, and establisheth them|transfert regna atque constituit]], as is declared in Daniel. [[3:13|thou hast laid bare his foundation even to the neck|Denudasti fundamentum ejus usque ad collum]], that is, thou wilt destroy them from the foundations; according to what is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 4:19|he shall burst them puffed up|Dirumpet inflatos]], [[Wis 4:19|and shall shake them from the foundations, and they shall be utterly laid waste|et eos a fundamentis suis commovebit, et usque ad supremum desolabuntur]].

paras.t: Maledicisti sceptris ejus, id est regno et potestatibus impiorum. Oculi enim Domini super regnum peccans, ut conterat illud. Quibus et dicitur in Osee : Ipsi regnaverunt, et non ex me. Vel intelligendum est de aeriis potestatibus et invisibilibus hostibus, venientibus ut turbo ad dispergendum nos, secundum quod ait Apostolus : Non est nobis colluctatio adversus carnem et sanguinem, sed adversus principes et potestates, contra spiritualia nequitiæ in cœlestibus. Exsultatio eorum sicut ejus qui devorat pauperem in abscondito. Invisibiles etenim hostes de animarum nostrarum ruina maxime gaudent, quemadmodum scriptum est in libro Psalmorum : Qui tribulant me, exsultabunt si motus fuero. Ideo orat vir sanctus : Neque irrideant me inimici mei. In Ecclesiastico quoque scriptum est : Domine Pater, ne derelinquas me, etc., et incidam in conspectu adversariorum meorum, et gaudeat inimicus meus. Nonne ergo miserrimi sunt, stulti et cæci, qui dæmonum inspirationi consentiunt vitiis inhærendo, qui aliud nihil nisi æternam eorum damnationem ac irrisionem exquirunt ?
paras.en: [[3:14|Thou hast cursed his sceptres|Maledicisti sceptris ejus]], that is, the kingdom and powers of the wicked. For [[Amos 9:8|the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom|Oculi enim Domini super regnum peccans]], to destroy it. To them it is also said in Osee: [[Osee 8:4|They have reigned, but not by me|Ipsi regnaverunt, et non ex me]]. Or it is to be understood of the powers of the air and the invisible enemies, [[3:14|them that came out as a whirlwind to scatter|venientibus ut turbo ad dispergendum]] us, according to what the Apostle says: [[Eph 6:12|our wrestling is not against flesh and blood; but against principalities and powers|Non est nobis colluctatio adversus carnem et sanguinem, sed adversus principes et potestates]], [[Eph 6:12|against the spirits of wickedness in the high places|contra spiritualia nequitiæ in cœlestibus]]. [[3:14|Their joy was like that of him that devoureth the poor man in secret|Exsultatio eorum sicut ejus qui devorat pauperem in abscondito]]. For the invisible enemies rejoice above all at the ruin of our souls, as it is written in the book of Psalms: [[Ps 12:5|They that trouble me, will rejoice when I am moved|Qui tribulant me, exsultabunt si motus fuero]]. Therefore the holy man prays: [[Ps 24:3|Neither let my enemies laugh at me|Neque irrideant me inimici mei]]. In Ecclesiasticus too it is written: [[Ecclus 23:1|O Lord, father|Domine Pater]], [[Ecclus 23:1|leave me not|ne derelinquas me]], etc., [[Ecclus 23:3|and I fall before my adversaries|et incidam in conspectu adversariorum meorum]], [[Ecclus 23:3|and my enemy rejoice over me|et gaudeat inimicus meus]]. Are they not, then, most wretched, foolish and blind, who consent to the prompting of the demons by clinging to vices, when the demons seek nothing else but their eternal damnation and mockery?

paras.t: Viam fecisti in mari equis tuis, id est electis : de quibus jam dictum est, Qui ascendes super equos tuos. Istis præparat Deus viam in hoc sæculo nequam, dando eis gratiam ambulandi per arctam viam quæ ducit ad vitam (hæc via, est divinorum custodia mandatorum, et eorum quæ jubet Ecclesia), in luto aquarum multarum, id est in carnali, mortali, immunda concupiscentiarum piscina, vel infra spurcitias vitiorum, ne in illis ambularent electi. Justum enim deduxit Dominus per vias rectas. Et Isaias : In manu, inquit, forti erudivit me Dominus, ne irem in via populi. Sed, ut in Jeremia legitur : Via impiorum erit quasi lubricum in tenebris ; impellentur et corruent in ea. Ideo gloriatur sanctus [David] in Domino, et ait : Eduxit me de lacu miseriæ, et de luto fæcis.
paras.en: [[3:15|Thou madest a way in the sea for thy horses|Viam fecisti in mari equis tuis]], that is, for the elect, of whom it has already been said: [[3:8|Who will ride upon thy horses|Qui ascendes super equos tuos]]. For these God prepares a way in this wicked world, giving them grace to walk along the narrow way that leads to life[[Matt 7:14||]] (this way is the keeping of the divine commandments and of what the Church commands), [[3:15|in the mud of many waters|in luto aquarum multarum]], that is, in the carnal, mortal, unclean pool of the concupiscences, or beneath the filth of vices, so that the elect should not walk in them. For the Lord [[Wis 10:10|conducted the just|Justum enim deduxit]] [[Wis 10:10|through the right ways|per vias rectas]] [in Wisdom it is Wisdom that does so; Denis has 'the Lord']. And Isaias: With a strong hand, he says, the Lord [[Is 8:11|hath taught me|erudivit me]], [[Is 8:11|that I should not walk in the way|ne irem in via]] of the people. But, as we read in Jeremias: The way of the wicked [[Jer 23:12|shall be as a slippery way in the dark|erit quasi lubricum in tenebris]]; [[Jer 23:12|they shall be driven on, and fall therein|impellentur et corruent in ea]]. Therefore holy David glories in the Lord and says: He [[Ps 39:3|brought me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs|Eduxit me de lacu miseriæ, et de luto fæcis]].

paras.t: Audivi, et conturbatus est venter meus. Hoc jam supra satis expositum est, etiam in principio cantici hujus. Ingrediatur putredo in ossibus meis, et subter me scateat : id est, nunc oro a te pro peccatis meis paternaliter castigari, et Christo pro me passo conformari : quemadmodum Jeremias deposcit, Corripe me, Domine, verumtamen non in furore tuo ; ut requiescam, id est, a cunctis miseriis liberer, in die tribulationis, id est hora mortis atque judicii ; ut ascendam ad populum accinctum nostrum, id est, de peregrinatione pertingam ad patriam, ad triumphantem Ecclesiam, ad milites illos victoriosissimos et beatos. Non enim sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad gloriam illam futuram.
paras.en: [[3:16|I have heard and my bowels were troubled|Audivi, et conturbatus est venter meus]]. This has already been explained sufficiently above, and also at the beginning of this canticle. [[3:16|Let rottenness enter into my bones, and swarm under me|Ingrediatur putredo in ossibus meis, et subter me scateat]]: that is, I pray now to be chastised by thee in a fatherly way for my sins, and to be conformed to Christ who suffered for me; as Jeremias asks: [[Jer 10:24|Correct me, O Lord, but yet|Corripe me, Domine, verumtamen]] [[Jer 10:24|not in thy fury|non in furore tuo]]; [[3:16|That I may rest|ut requiescam]], that is, that I may be freed from all miseries, [[3:16|in the day of tribulation|in die tribulationis]], that is, in the hour of death and of judgment; [[3:16|that I may go up to our people that are girded|ut ascendam ad populum accinctum nostrum]], that is, that I may pass from pilgrimage to the fatherland, to the Church triumphant, to those most victorious and blessed soldiers. For [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come|Non enim sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad gloriam illam futuram]].

paras.t: Hoc precor, quoniam inter homines vivere, periculosum mihi est. Ficus enim non florebit, id est, Ecclesia quantum ad plurimos, sine virtutum decore manebit. Etiam quidam, qui ex naturali dispositione mites et dulces sunt, bonitate suæ indolis abutentes, vitiis implicantur, vanitatibusque falluntur. Et non erit germen, id est fructus operum bonorum, in vineis, id est particularibus quibusdam Ecclesiis. Mentietur opus olivæ : id est, operatio eorum qui misericordes videntur, non erit vere meritoria, quia non ex caritate, sed vanitate procedens. Hoc accidit multis. Propter quod ait Salvator in Evangelio : Quum facis eleemosynam, nesciat sinistra tua quid faciat dextera tua, ut sit eleemosyna tua in abscondito.
paras.en: I pray for this because it is dangerous for me to live among men. [[3:17|For the fig tree shall not blossom|Ficus enim non florebit]], that is, the Church, as regards most of her members, will remain without the comeliness of virtues. Even some who by natural disposition are mild and sweet [as the fig is sweet], abusing the goodness of their temper, are entangled in vices and deceived by vanities. [[3:17|and there shall be no spring|Et non erit germen]], that is, the fruit of good works, [[3:17|in the vines|in vineis]], that is, in certain particular Churches. [[3:17|The labour of the olive tree shall fail|Mentietur opus olivæ]] [*mentietur*, literally 'shall lie']: that is, the work of those who seem merciful will not be truly meritorious, because it proceeds not from charity but from vanity. This happens to many. For which reason the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Matt 6:3|when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth|Quum facis eleemosynam, nesciat sinistra tua quid faciat dextera tua]], [[Matt 6:4|That thy alms may be in secret|ut sit eleemosyna tua in abscondito]].

paras.t: Vel, Mentietur opus olivæ : quoniam multi volunt aliis misereri atque succurrere, et propriis non miserentur neque subveniunt animabus, quas quotidie vitiis vulnerare non cessant, nec pœnitent, neque emendant. Ideo in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Miserere animæ tuæ placens Deo. Et Christus in Matthæo : Quid prodest homini, si universum mundum lucretur, animæ vero suæ detrimentum patiatur? Caritas ergo et pietas a se ipsis incipiant, et sic deriventur ad alios.
